Within the conventional designation of intrinsic nature belonging to the nature of conceptual construction, one speaks of the existence of the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*).
When a bodhisattva enters into the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), they eliminate both the grasper and the grasped within the nature of conventional designation;
therefore, it is said to be "equally equal.
The objective sphere traversed by non-conceptual wisdom is precisely the reality of the dependent nature, which is itself *tathatā* (suchness).
Among the seven kinds of suchness, the nature of dependence (paratantra-svabhāva) is also called suchness.
Bei states:
"This is based on the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) of suchness; therefore, its intrinsic nature is beyond words."
From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are conventionally designated as having intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
These two objects are equal and without distinction;
they are precisely the objective spheres traversed by the two kinds of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The Tripiṭaka masters also provide this same interpretation.
From here on is the second section, the detailed analysis according to the meaning,
which consists of five parts.
First, it clarifies that the true reality of what is realized is non-dual;
second, it clarifies that cultivating the superior resolve for emptiness constitutes the great skillful means;
third, it clarifies the modes of activity of the two types of wisdom that enter into the selflessness of phenomena and know the ineffable dharma.
The fourth [chapter] distinguishes how one who maintains control over the principle free from conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*) is able to cultivate correct practice.
The fifth extensively clarifies the ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpya-svabhāva*).

Regarding the initial passage which states: "Furthermore, it should be known that this established characteristic of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha-lakṣaṇa*) is that which is manifested by non-duality; as for the 'two' mentioned... up to... these are called 'non-existent,'" etc.
Jingyun: Initially, the four kinds of reality were summarized as a whole;
these are manifested by the non-duality of the dependent and the perfected natures.
This also explains non-duality.

Regarding the statement, "That which is called 'existence' here is that which has been grasped by the world for a long time," this refers to grasping at the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as being existent.
This is the superimposition of existence,

which is a form of denial. To say that things "do not exist" up to "are utterly non-existent" refers to the fact that one gives rise to pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita*) based upon those phenomena—

ranging from material forms up to nirvāṇa— which actually exist as the dependent (*paratantra*) and perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures, even though they lack any objective reality or intrinsic characteristics (*nimitta*) in their imagined nature.
To claim that both natures which serve as the basis for verbal expression are entirely non-existent is a denial through deprecation (*apavāda*).
To claim that because conventional designations and expressions function in dependence upon those [natures], they are all utterly non-existent, is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*).
Conventional designations and verbal expressions arise only by depending upon real dharmas;
yet, one slanders that which serves as their basis, claiming it to be entirely non-existent.
This is called "non-existence."
This refers to the slander of negation (*apavāda*).
That which was previously stated as "existent" is now stated as "non-existent"; thus, that which is "both existent and non-existent" is completely transcended.
This clarifies that within this chapter, the four types of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*) are entirely free from both the "existent" and the "non-existent" as previously described.
Regarding the statement that "the reality of things subsumed under the characteristics of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa) is called non-duality":
this brings forth the essence of that true non-dual dharma.
"Subsumed under the characteristics of phenomena" indicates that the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is the non-dual dharma.
The reality of suchness arises from that perfection as a non-dual dharma;
because it is non-dual, it is called the Middle Way, which is far removed from the two extremes, and it is also termed "unsurpassed."
Because it is devoid of these two kinds of meanings, it is free from the two extremes of augmentation and diminution,
and thus is called the Middle Way;
for this reason, it is also termed "unsurpassed."
Regarding the statement that the wisdom of all bodhisattvas is manifested by this truth of the path:
it is because the wisdom of all bodhisattvas still carries obscurations.
One gradually studies, cultivates, and realizes this reality.
Tai states:
"The purport of the central thesis here clarifies that both the dependent nature and the perfected nature are aspects of the meaning of reality."
This is precisely what is manifested by non-duality.
The term "duality" refers to the two [distinctions] established within the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are termed "existence."
For instance, as established in the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), self (*ātman*), and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*) is termed "non-existence.
Both this existence and non-existence are of the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

When a bodhisattva enters the contemplation of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya-vipaśyanā*), they distance themselves from both that which exists within this conceptual nature and that which does not exist.
The reality of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), which is subsumed under the characteristics of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa),
is called "non-duality.
This refers to the non-duality of existence and non-existence regarding the previously mentioned imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) and so forth.
Regarding the "two extremes":
[they are] existence and non-existence within the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Jì (基) says:
The meaning here is as follows:
all objects are fundamentally non-existent from the beginning;
yet, those who grasp at them falsely establish them as being "to be," and thus provisionally designate their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as existent.
This is the very root of the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) grasped by the world since beginningless time;
that is to say, because one gives rise to linguistic conceptualization (*nāma-vikalpa*) based on objects, [one continues] up to the point of conceiving the existence of nirvāṇa.
Such things as these exist through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
Because they are the objects of grasping and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they are said to "exist.
As for the statement that they do not exist:
This means that because the imagined nature of all phenomena such as form is designated as being without entity and without characteristics,
the verbal expressions upon which those designations depend— namely, the so-called "provisional dharmas"—
are entirely non-existent; for the basis of those names and words, being without entity and without characteristics, is utterly absent.
Because their basis does not exist, all such conceptualizations of form and so forth are entirely non-existent;
this is called "non-existence.
Thus, whether one conceives of existence or non-existence, both are merely parikalpita (imagined).
The Noble One [Nāgārjuna] designated this as the Middle Way.
Master Ce and others explain it, saying:
"One should know that this is precisely that which is revealed by non-duality."
To contemplate existence and non-existence as the true nature is this very reality,
which is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
It is also called "non-dual," and it is called "neither pure nor impure."
Therefore, the verse from the *Satyapariccheda* (Chapter on Reality) in the second fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states:
"It is neither existent nor non-existent;
it is neither identical nor different."
Neither arising nor ceasing;
neither increasing nor decreasing;
neither pure nor impure.
These five lack the characteristic of duality; this is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
The practitioner should know that its essence is "not existent."
Because the two characteristics—the imagined and the dependent—are non-existent;
because it is not non-existent, as the perfected characteristic does exist;
and because it is not "like" [the former].
Because the two characteristics— the imagined and the dependent— lack a single substantial entity,
they are not different;
for those two kinds of suchness lack any distinct essence.
It is neither arising nor ceasing because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It neither increases nor decreases because the *dharmadhātu* remains exactly as it is,
even when the two portions— the pure and the defiled— arise or cease.
It is not pure because its intrinsic nature is unstained and thus does not require purification;
it is not impure because adventitious defilements do not arise.
The Tripitaka Master’s commentary states:
This treatise says that what is called "the two" refers to the emergence of existence and non-existence as their essence.
"Existence" is precisely the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
"Non-existence" refers to the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Because the essence of suchness (*tathatā*) is free from existence and non-existence, it is said to be "non-dual," and so forth.
Second, in explaining how the cultivation of the resolute conviction in emptiness constitutes the great skillful means:
Master Ji’s commentary states:
Cultivating the wisdom of emptiness is the skillful means for awakening;
this is the emptiness of emptiness regarding the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
This is not the emptiness of non-existence as previously described.

Furthermore, this very wisdom is the single practice of all bodhisattvas; these three characters collectively clarify that the wisdom cultivated in emptiness is the skillful means (*upāya*) for awakening (*bodhi*).

Why is this? Because within the four [sections] that follow below, the first concerns the two practices of all bodhisattvas, from [the stage of] "below" up to the maturation of the Buddha-dharma and all sentient beings.
The first [phrase] clarifies that because of the wisdom of emptiness and existence, one does not cling to birth and death.
The second [phrase], "furthermore, being able to know birth and death as they truly are, up to the single practice of profound mental revulsion," consists of four characters.
Being clear about birth and death, they undergo many cycles of birth and death within it to teach and transform sentient beings.
They do not, through practices such as contemplating impermanence, become weary of or turn their backs on birth and death in order to seek entry into nirvana;
thus, they do not cling to nirvana.

Third, if bodhisattvas cannot understand birth and death as it truly is, up to and including the inability to accomplish the four practices for attaining the Buddha-dharma and [liberating] sentient beings—
this clarifies that those lacking wisdom frequently enter into birth and death and are unable to accomplish the Buddha-dharma and the welfare of sentient beings.
If there are those with wisdom who do not enter into birth and death and are well able to bring sentient beings to the accomplishment of the Buddha-dharma,
they "do not enter birth and death" because this distinguishes them from ordinary persons;
for unlike ordinary persons, they do not give rise to afflictions such as craving and thereby enter into birth and death.
That a bodhisattva does not enter [nirvāṇa] is due to wisdom;
they constantly abide in nirvāṇa.

Fourth, if bodhisattvas, regarding saṃsāra, feel profound revulsion through the mental application of impermanence and so forth, up to the three practices and four words leading to perfect enlightenment.
It clarifies that Bodhisattvas do not, like those of the Two Vehicles, weary of and turn their backs on birth and death to enter nirvana swiftly;
for they lack compassion.
Because Bodhisattvas possess compassion, they teach and transform sentient beings, not entering nirvana but remaining eternally within birth and death.
This immediately excludes the two vehicles (*dvayānaya*).
The preceding was the first interpretation;
the following is the second interpretation.

Furthermore, because bodhisattvas possess such a resolute conviction in emptiness, they maintain their initial correct understanding until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, provided they have not yet acquired great skillful means.
The second [section] covers and clarifies the preceding meaning and its interpretation.
Within the first [part], the "Correct Interpretation," there are three [subsections].
The first two provide a combined explanation.
The third and fourth [points] are each explained individually;
the first two are explained together.

The treatise says: "Furthermore, because bodhisattvas have practiced such resolute conviction in emptiness, they do not feel deep fear toward nirvāṇa, nor do they harbor excessive longing for nirvāṇa."
This is the first [reason]: because of the wisdom of emptiness, one does not fear nirvana while remaining within saṃsāra.
The second is that although one understands saṃsāra, one is able to enter nirvana, yet one does not harbor excessive longing for nirvana.
Because there is compassion;
this is the combined explanation of the first and second [stages].
How is this known?
This corresponds to the "knowledge" explained in the previous section.
Third, if bodhisattvas are deeply terrified of nirvana and even distance themselves from all pure understanding, it is because they possess afflictions (*kleśa*) and the like;
thus, being unskilled in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they fear nirvana and fail to give rise to the aspiration for it.
Consequently, they are unable to give rise to pure resolve toward the realm of nirvāṇa.
Due to this lack of wisdom, they cannot sever the cycle of birth and death—that is, they remain within the manifold realms of saṃsāra.
Fourth, if bodhisattvas dwell excessively in the aspiration for nirvāṇa to the point that they are unable to accomplish the Buddha-dharmas and the welfare of sentient beings;
Because they lack compassion, they deeply desire and long for nirvāṇa, seeking to enter it with haste;
consequently, they are unable to accomplish the qualities of a Buddha or the welfare of sentient beings.
Those who possess compassion do not delight in entering nirvāṇa.
Because they teach and transform sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death,
they do not cling to nirvana.
Thus far, the excellence of the wisdom that realizes emptiness has been correctly explained.
If the first two explanations are combined, there are three sections of text;
if considered by their meaning, there are four sections.
Herein, they are first designated as three sections.
The lower meaning is divided into four sections;
therefore, it says "the third, the fourth," and so forth.
From "one should know that herein" onwards, up to "and knowing the meaning of purity," [these constitute the sections].
In this regard, there are four [points].
First, because they lack the wisdom of emptiness,
they do not understand birth and death as they truly are.
This refers to the defiled mind that transmigrates through birth and death;
this is the inverse explanation.
In the combined explanation, the first point concerns not fearing nirvāṇa.
Second, if one becomes weary of birth and death through the contemplation of impermanence, one will swiftly enter nirvāṇa.
This is the reverse interpretation;
it corresponds to the second point within the combined interpretation, which also states that one does not have much aspiration or delight for nirvāṇa.
Third, if due to a lack of wisdom one feels deep-seated fear toward nirvāṇa,
one will be unable to fulfill the provisions for realizing nirvāṇa and will thus remain perpetually within saṃsāra.
This is the inverse explanation.
Above, the third [point] was the distancing from all pure resolute convictions.
Fourth, if one lacks compassion and dwells frequently in the aspiration for nirvāṇa, one will then very quickly enter parinirvāṇa.
This is the inverse explanation.
Above, the fourth section concerned sentient beings who are unable to accomplish the Buddha-dharma;
now, concluding this inverse explanation, the treatise states: "These bodhisattvas lack the great skillful means for realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The third section below explains the four meanings;
they can be understood by applying the underlying principle to the text.
Alternatively, the first [section] correctly elucidates the four meanings.
This is the general establishment of the thesis.
It should be understood that within this, the subsequent section provides a reverse explanation that reinterprets the meaning of what preceded it.
Within this reinterpretation, there are two parts.
The first part provides a preliminary explanation of the four meanings;
the second part offers a formal exposition of the four meanings.
Jing says:
First, it briefly clarifies that the wisdom realizing reality (*tattvārtha-jñāna*) is the great skillful means (*upāya*) capable of attaining bodhi.
Second, it extensively distinguishes four skillful means, providing two successive detailed explanations.
Within the first of these sections:
First, it is explained that there are two skillful means regarding saṃsāra;
subsequently, it is explained that one possesses two skillful means regarding nirvāṇa.
Within the former, the explanation is direct, while in the latter, it is inverse.
The same applies to the middle [period] thereafter.

Vasubandhu, taking this intended meaning, employed it in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*: "By means of these two skillful means—one being thorough comprehension of the suffering of saṃsāra so as to be able to enter it constantly, and the other being knowledge of the bliss of nirvāṇa without seeking it too hastily."
These are the two skillful means. Tái says:
"Furthermore, because bodhisattvas cultivate such resolute conviction in emptiness, they do not feel deep fear toward nirvāṇa, nor do they harbor excessive longing for nirvāṇa."
If, according to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one conceives of a real nirvana that severs the body and consciousness,
then ordinary beings will feel fear when they perceive a self. Now,
the Bodhisattva enters into the non-existence of a self within phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), realizing that the body, consciousness, and nirvana were fundamentally non-existent.
Furthermore, the nirvāṇa realized by Bodhisattvas does not sever the body and wisdom.
Because they rely upon the two natures—the dependent and the real—they do not give rise to fear.
They know that the suffering grasped by the mind within saṃsāra is originally empty by its very nature.
Since one does not feel extreme revulsion toward saṃsāra,
one likewise does not harbor excessive longing for nirvāṇa.
Third, it clarifies the modes of activity of the two types of wisdom that realize the ineffable dharma by entering into the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya).
First is the brief exposition, next the detailed explanation, and finally the conclusion.
Jing says:

"The phrase 'because one is able to deeply enter the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), even down to the slightest categories that might give rise to conceptual discrimination'..."
One thoroughly penetrates the ineffable intrinsic nature of both the dependent and the perfected;
apart from these two kinds of ineffable phenomena, there is no further subtle phenomenon or minor category that can give rise to conceptual discrimination.
This immediately reveals that apart from these two natures, the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is ultimately non-existent.
The phrase "merely grasping its object, it functions only with respect to the referent" clarifies the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of these two types of wisdom.
Subsequent knowledge apprehends only the dependently originated entity, yet it does not form the thought,
"This is a mere entity.
Non-conceptual wisdom apprehends only suchness, yet it does not form this thought.
"It is solely True Suchness (tathatā),
for it functions in common with its object while remaining free from conceptual discrimination. Ce says:
There are three different interpretations among the Western masters.
One says:
it refers exclusively to the dependent-arising cognition that takes its object as its causal basis.
It takes only suchness as its object and possesses wisdom that has suchness as its object;
this pair refers to both types of wisdom.
As for the statement, "one does not form the thought that 'this thing is suchness,'" it means:
The aspect of the activity of the two knowledges is explained as follows:
conventional knowledge, when taking [phenomena] as its object, does not form the thought,
"This is merely a thing."
The wisdom that takes suchness as its object does not form the thought,
"This is only suchness. However, for one who practices in accordance with the meaning, both types of wisdom are joined together.
Because this is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it does not give rise to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) but merely takes its objective essence as its object.
One interpretation states:
"That which grasps only the particular phenomenon (*vastu*) is the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*)."
One does not form the thought, "This is the objective aspect (grāhyāṃśa)," nor "This is the subjective aspect (grāhakāṃśa) which is mere suchness (tathatāmātra).
One does not form the thought that "mere suchness operates solely upon objects."
The two knots [of the self-witnessing aspect] function with respect to the meaning of the seeing aspect;
the seeing aspect functions with respect to the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).
A third interpretation states:
Regarding "only grasping its phenomenal aspect," this refers to conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) prior to the grounds.
Regarding "only grasping the true suchness (*tathatā*)," [this refers to ultimate wisdom].
The passage beginning with "As in the stage of application,
one contemplates suchness and does not form such thoughts" refers to the non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) from the first bhūmi upward.
Tai said:
"Regarding self-nature, one realizes that there is not the slightest phenomenon upon which discrimination can arise;
regarding meaning, one realizes that there is not the slightest category upon which discrimination can arise."
Next, the aspects of the two types of wisdom are extensively analyzed.
First, the aspects of correct wisdom are clarified;
next, the aspects of subsequent wisdom are clarified.
The concluding summary of the two types of wisdom of a bodhisattva states that both are accomplished by relying on the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena through skillful means.
The first part says: "In this way, the bodhisattva... until attaining the most excellent equanimity."
Jingyun: True Suchness (tathatā) pervades all phenomena.
When fundamental wisdom functions within true suchness, [it is as follows].
Regarding all phenomena as perfectly equal,
one attains the supreme equanimity through the realization of the equality of suchness within the locus of all phenomena;
this is further explained as non-conceptual wisdom associated exclusively with equanimity.
As for the term "Ground of Supreme Joy" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*),
it refers to the joy of mind arising from the subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) after emerging from meditative equipoise.
T'ai says:
Both the dependent nature and the perfected nature are termed "ultimate reality" (paramārtha).
Among the seven kinds of suchness, both are true suchness (tathatā).
Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
Dependence on others is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
From this point downward, the text specifically clarifies the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) of the realization of true reality;
for within all phenomena, there is neither a grasper nor that which is grasped.
It speaks again of equality:
because one observes with the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness) as it truly is, one possesses the mind of equal concentration and wisdom in all circumstances; this refers to concentration (*samādhi*).
"Seeing" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*).

Because it realizes suchness (*tathatā*) and is free from the extremes of sinking and floating through both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom, it is called "supreme equanimity" (*upekṣā*).
Master Ji said:
When a bodhisattva attains the vision of equality and attains a mind of equality, they are able to attain the most supreme equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Some say that this equanimity,
which is first attained upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), refers specifically to the equanimity of sensation (*vedanopekṣā*).
Not so. Regarding the functional mode (*ākāra*) of the capacity of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
Jing said:
This consists of six points:
first, by relying on this equanimity, one is able to swiftly accomplish proficiency in all fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) and all skills (*kauśalya*);
second, one attains the power of great mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), not becoming arrogant because of such skill or being stingy with it.
Third, while within the great suffering of the cycle of birth and death, one becomes capable of increasing the growth of bodhi;
fourth, the arrogance of seeking noble status gradually ceases;
fifth, one attains superior wisdom and abandons the mind that finds it difficult to help others.
"The six functions gradually increase and turn back one's own wholesome [roots].
Tai [Zongyi] says:
"As for the statement 'the attainment of wisdom is preeminent, up to the point where the profound mind abandons [them],' it refers to this."
Ordinary persons, having attained only a small measure of wisdom, engage in challenging, disputing, and litigating with others.
Bodhisattvas are not like this;

having attained superior wisdom, they redouble their efforts to abandon challenges, enmities, and disputes toward others—even when faced with the commission of transgressions or the manifestation of prohibited conduct.

Therefore, from "all [these]" onwards is the third section, which concludes that all Buddhas of the three times attain bodhi by relying on the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*).
The fourth section distinguishes how one can correctly practice by upholding the principle of non-proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
First there is the general summary, then the specific details, and finally the conclusion.
Within the specific details, these are the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
The first five perfections are easily understood.
In the sixth [chapter], *Prajñā*, it first clarifies non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*),
meaning that one accomplishes the wisdom of ultimate reality for the sake of one's own future parinirvāṇa.
Next, it clarifies that subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) has four aspects.
First, to revere those with merit;
second, to have compassion for those with faults;
third, to be kind toward one's enemies.
Fourth is the ability to repay kindness:
if one has the power and resources such as wealth and goods, one should provide a corresponding recompense;
if one lacks the power and resources, [one should instead offer service].
When someone comes to request [something], one immediately acts on their behalf without contradicting their wishes,
so as to let them know that one truly lacks the power [to fulfill the request].
Fifth, within the extensive explanation of the ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpya-svabhāva*), there are four sections.
First, the text correctly distinguishes the ineffable intrinsic nature;
second, it cites scriptural teachings to establish this proof;
third, it clarifies the intention behind the Buddhas' employment of verbal expression.
The fourth section clarifies that regarding teachings which transcend words, eight types of conceptual discrimination arise.
Within this, first there is the question, next the answer, and finally the conclusion.
As for the statement, "By what principle should one know that all phenomena have a self-nature that transcends words? it is as follows:
Ordinary beings must rely on words to know phenomena;
by investigating words, they can grasp their meaning and thereby attain understanding.
As the Master of the Treatise stated above:
Regarding all phenomena, since their ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpya-svabhāva*) is beyond expression, they are devoid of any form or appearance.
On what basis, then, can one know that an ineffable intrinsic nature exists?
The answer has two parts.
First, the establishment of the orthodox teaching;
second, the refutation of heterodox attachments from the passage "If, regarding all phenomena... and below.
Regarding the former, Jing says:
The intent of this passage is as follows:
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess non-conceptual wisdom that knows phenomena beyond words;
other ordinary beings, however, possess only wisdom that conforms to verbal expression and are unable to know phenomena that transcend words.
Now, for the sake of those who rely on verbal expressions, one uses inference based on meaning to enable them to know that there exist those ineffable dharmas.
Just as ordinary people today raise their minds to take objects as conditions, giving rise to speech and grasping, they are all deluded regarding the two truths.
Just as verbal expressions arise for the sake of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
one clings to the existence of a substantial essence of conventional truth according to those words,
and clings to it according to those expressions.
Although conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is non-existent, it is not that there is nothing to which one is deluded;

it is a conventional truth that transcends words. Just as verbal expressions are employed for the sake of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one may cling to the existence of an essence of ultimate truth according to those words.
Emotional attachment follows conventional expression;
although ultimate truth is non-existent, it is not that there is nothing to which one might be deluded. Ultimate truth is beyond words.
If there were no delusion regarding the two truths that transcend words, [there would be no need for this teaching].
That is to say, insentient things possess the grasping of the two truths as they are conceptually constructed;

now, by citing the fact that the objects of conceptual construction lack intrinsic nature, it is demonstrated that there is something delusively perceived which is beyond verbal expression within the two truths.
Regarding the statement that "all phenomena are conventionally established with respect to their own-characteristics, up to and including the absence of intrinsic nature":
this refers to the adherence to the nature of phenomena based on words;
it is not that they exist, but rather that there are only verbal designations.
Nor is it the case that [the nature of phenomena] is separate from those words that reach the realm of expression.
The opponent offers this defense:
"Although the nature of the expressed phenomenon does not exist within the expressive words,"
What prevents one from saying that there is something else expressed apart from words, which is thus the range of verbal activity?
Therefore, he further refutes this by stating:
"Nor is it the case that there is a self-nature existing apart from words which is the range of verbal activity."
This point will be refuted by the proponent himself later in the text.
The opponent further states:
"The term 'fundamental' (mūla) refers to the dharma-nature (dharmatā)."
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not existent;
it should therefore be said that its nature is non-existent.
For this reason, it is further stated now:
Thus, these phenomena do not possess an intrinsic nature as it is expressed by words;
yet, they are not entirely non-existent either.
Although the entities grasped according to words do not exist,
it cannot be said that the conventional expressions themselves are entirely non-existent.
Furthermore, the opponent says:
Since even the phenomena expressed by words do not exist in themselves, the phenomena that transcend words should likewise not exist;
therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "In this way, they do not exist, yet it is not the case that they are entirely non-existent."
The nature that conforms to verbal expression is neither existent in this way, nor is it the case that the ineffable intrinsic nature is entirely non-existent.
How could it exist? Since it is not entirely non-existent...
How can it exist? It is said that it exists in such a way by being free from superimposition (*samāropa*), and so forth, up to "existing in this manner.
This means that if one is free from the two types of grasping—namely, increase and decrease—with respect to the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).

Therefore, it is said that "existence" refers to the superimposition of existence upon that which is utterly non-existent— the parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature)— and the denial of existence regarding that which truly exists—
the paratantra- and pariniṣpanna-svabhāvas (dependent and perfected natures).
Because of these two types of false attachments—namely, superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*)—one cannot realize the existence of the ineffable reality (*nirabhilāpya-dharma*).
Only when one is free from both superimposition and denial can one realize its existence.
Below, it is shown that because the two types of knowledge are free from superimposition and denial, the existence of the two natures (*dvaya-svabhāva*) is known.
Therefore, it is said that this very thing is the ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) of all phenomena;
one should know that it is exclusively the objective sphere of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*),
and that it does not exist in relation to the erroneously imagined phenomena (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Therefore, the other two natures are both termed "ultimate" (paramārtha).
The perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is the object of non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna);
the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), which arises from causes and conditions, is the object of subsequent non-conceptual wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna).
Therefore, it is said in general that the ultimate intrinsic nature is exclusively the objective domain of non-conceptual wisdom.
Tai [Xuanzang] says:
"It is like the Sarvāstivāda and other schools."
When one sees colors such as blue or yellow with the eye, it is called "what is seen by the eye," and these colors—blue, yellow, and so forth—are described accordingly.

This continues up to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) taking *nirvāṇa* as its object; following what is perceived by the mental consciousness, it is said that *nirvāṇa*, which is the cessation of dispersion, possesses a determinate nature.
Therefore, all phenomena can be described as the limits of the objects perceived by one's own mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*).
This is not the case in the Mahāyāna.
For example, when visual consciousness perceives form (*rūpa*):
Visual consciousness is a cognition of direct perception (*pramāṇa*).
The object is designated as the objective range of visual consciousness;
thus, one directly realizes that the form of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is inexpressible.

Furthermore, the specific limits of the form-object apprehended by the simultaneously arising conceptualizing consciousness (*sahaja-vikalpa-manovijñāna*) cannot be described in terms of its color or appearance; therefore,
that which is known through direct perception (*pramāṇa*) is called "the dharma" (*dharma*),
wherein both the means of cognition and the object of cognition are ineffable.
Following visual consciousness, mental consciousness arises and begins to discriminate:
"I see forms with my eye," and it describes what is seen by the eye as blue, yellow, and so forth;
this continues up until the description of the subsequent knowledge that arises after the untainted knowledge of cessation (*anāsrava-nirodha-jñāna*).
I say that I speak of nirvāṇa from within nirvāṇa; therefore,
when I speak of all phenomena as being form, and so forth up to nirvāṇa,
none of these accord with what is known through direct valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is able to provisionally designate the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form, up to and including the provisional designation of the specific characteristics of nirvāṇa.
Regarding the question posed above, by what principle should one understand that all phenomena possess a nature beyond words?
The answer below states:
all phenomena are provisionally established with their own characteristics;
they are either called "form" or called "feeling."
One should know that everything up to and including nirvāṇa is merely a conventional designation.
The specific characteristics of all phenomena, even those known through direct perception, are inexpressible.
They do not possess an intrinsic nature, nor are they the domain of such verbal expressions.
Furthermore, the Sarvāstivādins and others assert that all things exist by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The Vaiśeṣikas maintain the six categories (*padārtha*);
because of the fourth category, "existence" (*sattā*), they hold that all phenomena are established as existent.
This "existence" (astitva) possesses its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva) distinct from all phenomena;
therefore, an intrinsic nature is established separately outside the essence of phenomena.
Such intrinsic natures as those posited by the Hīnayāna and non-Buddhists are all merely the domain of verbal expression.
This is the domain of verbal expression;
since it is not that which is grasped by those [grasping],
it is said that there is no intrinsic nature.
It is not that, according to the Sarvāstivāda, phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
rather, that which is expressed by words is the domain of speech.
Nor is it the case that there exists an intrinsic nature or the like apart from those [phenomena].
For the Vaiśeṣika, there is no self-nature (svabhāva) existing apart from the essence of those phenomena;
rather, this [self-nature] is the range of speech and the objective domain of speech.
This refers to that which is free from the false attachment to what is non-existent through superimposition (samāropa).
The first explanation is largely the same as that of Master Jing.
The second explanation further states:
"To be free from the attachment to real existence through superimposition is itself the nature of reality."
To be free from the attachment to the real existence of things through denial is precisely the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
"Existing in this way" means that the reality of the dependent nature is what is meant by "existence."
The intent of the reply is fully set forth as follows:
it concerns the abandonment of the false attachment to the existence of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) apart from the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva),
and the abandonment of the false attachment to the non-existence of the suchness (tathatā) that is the basis of the dependent nature.
Thus, being free from existence and free from non-existence, yet existing within non-existence,
this is the ultimate essence and characteristic of all phenomena;
it is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the true suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness as explained in the *Dharmadharmatāvibhaṅga*.
Jizang says:
The treatise asks by what principle one knows the ineffable nature [of phenomena].
In the response, it states that while all dharmas are conventionally established with their own characteristics, this does not mean that everything is utterly non-existent.
In this context, there are two parts to the refutation of attachment.
First, the passage from "even these words" up to "the range of words" and "the domain of words" restates the two external positions.
Second, from "thus, all these phenomena lack intrinsic nature" onwards, there is a further refutation of the external positions to establish one's own school.
The second conception refers to the fact that all phenomena are provisionally established with their own characteristics, and so on,
up to being merely conventionally posited.
They do not possess intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
This is not as the outsiders (*bāhya*) claim;
for just as the designating name and the designated object are both conventionally established, the name does not correspond to the object.
Regarding the names and designations as they are grasped and conceptualized, which refer to and apprehend the objects they signify:
these objects are merely conventionally established and lack intrinsic nature;
thus, their essence is said to be non-existent.
Since it has been established that the names designated do not correspond to their objects,
and once it is determined that the objects so designated do not exist,
the opponent shifts his argument as follows.
Therefore, the second treatise states:
"Nor does it exist as a self-nature separate from those;
it is that which is traversed by speech and is the objective sphere of speech."
Since the names that express do not correspond to the referents they express,
it follows that within those expressive names there is a combination of the entities such as form and so forth;
this is what is called "correspondence," and it is the objective sphere traversed by such expression.
Therefore, the Master of the Treatise refutes this.

He also refutes the view that, apart from the essence of the signified object, there exists a separate intrinsic nature of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) which is the range of speech and the objective domain of words.

This means that when names and so forth are conventionally established, they exist upon the very forms and other phenomena that are their referents; thus, the sense of being the objective domain of such linguistic expression is called the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because it is imagined as the referent corresponding to the expression and is the objective domain of that expression.
To say that form and so forth are conjoined with names— that is, conjoined within the name—
and that this is the range of speech or the objective domain of speech, is not correct.
Although that which is conceptualized is not real, its false nature is not non-existent.
If an outsider were to argue that since the referent is non-existent, then all previously mentioned intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) and so forth must likewise be non-existent; [we respond as follows].
Therefore, the Master of the Treatise states in the second chapter:
"Thus, these phenomena do not possess an intrinsic nature as it is expressed by words."
Nor is it the case that everything is utterly non-existent;
for even that which is expressed by the term "thoroughly imagined" (parikalpita)—namely, the phenomena said to lack intrinsic nature—is not itself utterly non-existent.

To say that there is a dependent, illusory object which is not non-existent is to refute the first type of extreme view: the conceptualization that the referent of a designation exists as an external object.
Likewise, to say that it is neither existent nor entirely non-existent is [to refute the second type].
Regarding the externalist claim that speech and names conjoin with cognition to designate objects,
these do not exist apart from speech.
As for the preceding statement "it is not," this means it is non-existent.
Now, when it is stated that such an apprehended composite does not exist,
this is because the dependent nature and false imagination still persist;
nor is it the case that everything is utterly non-existent.
Another explanation:
From the beginning up to "merely conventionally established and lacking intrinsic nature," this clarifies the refutation of externalist views.
For example, it is as when the dharma signified by a name corresponds to its own designating name.
One should know that all these phenomena, such as form and so forth, are merely conventional designations and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is said that the entity as it is conceptualized is non-existent.
Once the opponent sees that the referent is non-existent, [the argument proceeds].
Because it is not designated by that name, one consequently resorts to the following calculation:
if the phenomenon referred to by such a name is not designated by the name "form," then there must exist a self-nature (svabhāva) distinct from and external to the form that is so referred to.
This statement— that what is traversed by speech and what constitutes the domain of speech exists as a self-nature distinct from those [objects]—
is now refuted by the Master of the Treatise.
Therefore, he states that it is not the case that there is a self-nature existing apart from them which serves as the domain traversed by speech.
Although one may posit "is" or "is not," these are not what is reckoned to exist;
for the very essence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and so forth is neither existent nor non-existent.
As the treatise states: "Thus, these phenomena do not possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as it is expressed by words, yet they are not entirely non-existent either."
Just as previously reckoned and as expressed by words, there are no phenomena possessing intrinsic nature;
that which is grasped does not exist,
just like the provisional designation of names and conventions based upon dependent phenomena.
Furthermore, this dharma is not entirely non-existent;
it cannot be devoid of the dependent nature and so forth,
for it is not the case that it lacks intrinsic nature.
This refers to the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
It does not mean that everything described by words is entirely non-existent;
rather, it refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and so forth.
It is not only that the dependent nature, which is beyond verbal expression, exists;
rather, even those non-existent phenomena that are grasped at exist within the sphere of deluded cognition.
Therefore, it is also not the case that everything is utterly non-existent.
Therefore, the second treatise states:
"In this way, it is neither non-existent nor is it the case that everything is utterly non-existent.
Having thus clarified above that what was previously conceptualized as non-existent is not so, while the dependent and perfected natures are indeed existent.
Therefore, the treatise poses the question:
"What is existence?
In response, one should state that it is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) which, when designated as "known," is beyond verbal expression.

Now, because we take up the wisdom that is capable of illumination, it is said that this is exclusively the objective domain of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); furthermore, its subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is also able to take true phenomena as its object without error.
Now, because this takes up the primary condition, it relies solely upon non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
[Tang] Yuanze says:
"The statement 'from the imputed self-nature of all phenomena' up to 'the absence of self-nature'..."
This means that based upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one eliminates the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, it is not the case that there exists a self-nature (*svabhāva*) separate from that which serves as the objective domain of speech.
The intent of this refutation is as follows:
Apart from that dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) which arises from conditions, there is no separate, substantially grasped imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva);
it is like saying that "self-nature" is the range of speech and the objective domain of speech.
The passage beginning with "In this way, regarding all these phenomena" clarifies that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) exists upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Within this, there are two parts.
First, it clarifies that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which is revealed by the absence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) upon the dependent nature, does exist.
Second, regarding the passage "In this way, they do not exist," and so forth, the question-and-answer section distinguishes the reason why the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) exists.
It states: "While these phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in this way, what has been said does not mean that everything is utterly non-existent."
This means that upon the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), there is no real, pervasive, imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) as expressed by words;
nor does it mean that the suchness (tathatā) manifested by the dependent nature is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).

As stated above, "because it does not exist," and so forth, this is the second explanation regarding the reason why the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) exists upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
This section contains two parts:
first, restating the preceding point as a question.
"In this way, 'it does not exist' refers to the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
'nor is it entirely non-existent' refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The phrase 'the two, namely, having abandoned superimposition,' and so forth, is the explanation."
This refers to being free from the false attachment to what is non-existent as real, up to the point of [denying] the ultimate intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*).
The intended meaning is that,
within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one is free from the false attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as being truly existent.

Furthermore, when one is free from the false attachment to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and realizes that the suchness (*tathatā*) upon which it depends is truly devoid of such delusion—
thus being free from both existence and non-existence—
that very state is the ultimate perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
This refers to the suchness (tathatā) manifested by the non-existence of both person and phenomena;
it should be understood that this is exclusively the objective domain of non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna).
This concludes the clarification of the ineffable intrinsic nature.
The above establishes the correct doctrine (*siddhānta*).
From here below is the second section, which refutes erroneous attachments (*mithyā-grāha*). Ji says:
The following section further refutes the externalist tenets.
It contains two parts:
first, the refutation of the Hīnayāna adherence to the existence of conceptual proliferation (*parikalpita*) as speech that follows linguistic conventions.

Regarding the second [point], there are two types of persons. First, the refutation of those who, as beginners in the Mahāyāna, have wrongly grasped emptiness (*ayoniśa-śūnyatā-grāha*) and slander all dharmas that are beyond verbal expression as being non-existent.
Within this first section, there are two parts;
the first consists of three successive repetitions that refute [the opponent] extensively through reasoning.
The section beginning with "Secondly, by these causes and conditions" concludes the refutation of the analogy and its universal application.
Within the preceding [section], the first part consists of the primary refutation of the established thesis,
while the subsequent two parts refute the opponent's attempts at defense.
Furthermore, these three successive points reveal three fallacies:
first, the fallacy of multiple entities corresponding to a single name;
second, the fallacy of the non-existence of an entity prior to its naming.
The third [point] clarifies the error in the previous [position].
In the first section, Jìngyún states:
"If, regarding all phenomena and all things, whenever verbal expressions arise, those phenomena and those things possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."
This is the formal statement of the position.
The followers of the Hīnayāna establish that names are capable of summoning dharmas;
therefore, they maintain that the substantial entity of a dharma exists in accordance with verbal expression.
In this way, if a single dharma or a single thing were to possess numerous intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*),
then just as a single worldly dharma has many names, so too would there be a nature of a dharma for every dharma that is spoken of.
The essence of phenomena (dharmasvabhāva) should correspond to the multiplicity of its verbal designations; for instance, a single eye has many names,
being called either "the eye" or "that which sees."
In this way, a single eye would have multiple entities corresponding to its many names.
Master Vasubandhu, taking this point into account, states in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*:
"If a name were to definitively express [its object]..."
"Because names are many and entities are many.
As for the question, "Why [is it] up to 'because they express'?
this explains the fault that the nature of phenomena (dharmasvabhāva) would become as numerous as their names.

Regarding the statement, "Nor can a definitive expression through various conventional designations be found, nor even through any other conventional designations," the Master [Vasubandhu] previously raised this objection:
if intrinsic nature (svabhāva) existed simply by virtue of the arising of verbal expressions.
This means that a single dharma possesses multiple names;
if one were to follow the literal expression of these multiple names, there would have to be as many distinct entities.
Fearing that an external opponent might raise such an objection, [the author] says:
I have already sealed this by stating that if there were many names, there would consequently be many entities.
Therefore, it is refuted here:
nor can it be established that there are multiple entities corresponding to the various conventional designations used to express them.
That is to say, when one speaks metaphorically of "the eye" in its various singular or plural forms, there exists a distinct entity called the eye;
it is not that other faculties are designated by the name "seeing.
This applies even up to the case where, according to whatever name one uses for "the eye," there exists a corresponding entity of the eye, and so forth.
Therefore, regarding the statement that all conventional designations—whether complete or incomplete—even possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*):
according to each of your three preceding propositions, as soon as a verbal expression arises, it must possess an intrinsic nature.
However, although that single dharma follows many verbal designations, it possesses no manifold intrinsic natures (svabhāva).
This leads one to know that all conventional designations and conceptual constructions possess [only] their own [conventional] intrinsic natures;
thus, a single dharma has multiple names, each corresponding to its own [designation].
A single dharma has but a single name; thus, its names are not complete.
It is asked:
In the Mahāyāna, every single moment possesses both the aspect of the object (*nimitta*) and the aspect of the perceiver (*darśana*).
Thus, upon a single substantial entity that is the eye, there are numerous names;

according to each individual name, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) discriminates and is able to produce a portion of the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) of the eye, arising in accordance with that name.
This is precisely because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) follows multiplicity without any fault.
How can you raise the objection: "If the nature of phenomena exists in accordance with verbal expression, then is it not a fault that there are multiple entities corresponding to those many names?"
The commentary states:
According to the Hīnayāna, all dharmas established therein are expressible in words;
therefore, they maintain that all dharmas possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) as they are designated and summoned by names.
According to its essential nature, we now raise difficulties regarding that nature following its various names; we shall not discuss the aspect of the object (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Within the Hīnayāna schools, it is said:
The image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) is comprised within the cognitive objects of the practice of understanding;
therefore, one cannot speak of it as being manifold according to its name based on the image-aspect of the mind.
This is because, within the Mahāyāna, the doctrine of consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātra) is established by positing both the image-aspect and the seeing-aspect (darśana-bhāga).
When the mind of that Hīnayāna practitioner takes an object as its focal point, the mental aspect (ākāra) is not the actual perceiver;
rather, it is the reflection of the essential nature (svabhāva) of that objective realm.
Therefore, what is here explained—both the establishment and the refutation—concerns only the essential nature.
You claim that the intrinsic nature exists in accordance with names;
however, this entails the fault that if there are many names, there must also be many entities.
Tai says:
It is said that if one were to posit an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) regarding the entities of all phenomena,
it would be as stated in the *Nyāyapraveśa*: "Sound" is the subject (*dharmin*),
while "impermanence," "emptiness," and "selflessness" are the properties (*dharma*).
"Phenomena" refers to the phenomena of existing dharmas.
For example, as stated regarding eye-consciousness, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) abiding in form is an ineffable dharma that cannot be expressed in words;
following the arising of eye-consciousness, mental consciousness subsequently engages in conceptual discrimination.
Or one forms a perception of form, such as perceptions of blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth;
following the arising of verbal expressions, one speaks of perceptions of blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, and so forth,
and in accordance with those verbal expressions, various characteristics manifest.
Just as an echo arises in dependence upon sound, so too,
because of verbal expression, the various things and phenomena within the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Therefore,
it is said that "names are what is conceived by the mental consciousness."
"If all phenomena and all things possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) corresponding to their verbal designations"—
this is the restatement of the opponent's position.
In the subsequent refutation, the first part clarifies the many faults of names.
The second [point] states that although many errors have been mentioned, it is sufficient to follow one;
this means that what follows below directly exposes the contradictory nature of their tenets,
thereby summarizing the refutation.
If it is complete,
it is because it establishes numerous conventional designations through its formulation;
if it is incomplete, [it is for the following reason].
In the second section on the "Multitude," there is but one definitive point.
From this point onward, I have re-examined the Sanskrit manuscript to establish the certainty;
one must not follow the text of the old version and treat it as a divergent school.
Jizang says:
"That which is the 'dharma' refers to the teaching that expresses [the truth], such as the scriptures;
that which is the 'matter' (vastu) refers to the essential meaning expressed, such as the underlying reality."
"Having substance" (yǒutǐ) refers generally to the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena;
"having parts" (yǒufēn) analyzes the distinct divisions of phenomena.
This is the explanation according to the second alternative interpretation.
That is to say, the external opponent offers this defense:
"What I previously stated— that the various phenomena such as form (rūpa) possess only a single essence according to conventional designation (prajñapti)—
does not mean that they can be said to possess multiple essences according to their names."
Nevertheless, because there must exist a real entity corresponding to conventional designations,
he restates the opponent's defense, saying:
"Furthermore, as previously stated regarding form and all other phenomena..."
If one were to hold that there is an intrinsic nature according to conventional designations,
this refers to the Hīnayāna school's position that each and every phenomenon of the three times has its own respective name from among the three times used to designate it.
This means that the substance of the dharma exists prior to its being expressed by a name.

Since the teachers of the Hīnayāna previously established their thesis that all dharmas, such as form (*rūpa*), exist only in accordance with conventional designation (*prajñapti*), [the author] takes up this statement to refute it;
furthermore, he refutes it through both progressive and regressive analysis in the latter two sections.
The initial refutation concerns the existence of a substantial entity (dharmatva) corresponding to conventional designations;
the subsequent refutation addresses the prior claim that there are entities such as "form" which are subsequently expressed by names.
The present passage constitutes the first refutation, specifically a refutation of the attempted defense against that initial point.
In the principles of the world, a thing must first exist before its name is established.
Since you have previously asserted that phenomena such as form exist only in accordance with words, these phenomena would depend upon words for their existence;
thus, at the time when they have not yet been spoken of, they should lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If things lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) prior to being expressed in speech,
does this not contradict your claim that future phenomena already possess an essence (*bhāva*) beforehand and subsequently arise from conditions?
[The opponent] asks:
If it were indeed devoid of intrinsic nature prior to verbal expression,
what further fault would there be?
Next, the following objection is raised:
If it were not possible for conventional designations to be established to express things that lack intrinsic nature,
then it would be illogical to establish names for things that do not yet exist as entities;
and it would likewise be illogical to establish names for things that lack an entity.
Regarding the statement that it is unreasonable for a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) to express something because there is no destination [for it]:
if a name has not yet been applied, the entity (*dharmatā*) does not exist; and if the entity does not exist, it is impossible to apply a name to it.
Since there is no such thing as a name,
it would be unreasonable for the essence of worldly phenomena to exist merely by following conventional designations;
thus says Ji.
Since you claim that names correspond to their referents such that what is named is precisely that which is designated,
it follows that prior to the establishment of the conventional designation, the object signified by that name would lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because things exist only in accordance with their names,
that thing does not exist when its name has not yet arisen.
Since that thing is already non-existent prior to the arising of its name, [it cannot be established].
Furthermore, it is unreasonable for names that function as designators to manifest their referents.
Since names used as mere designations do not exist [inherently],
it is likewise unreasonable for the phenomena that are the referents to possess an intrinsic nature corresponding to those designating names.
He refutes it by turning it back upon itself.
In the third section, Jing says:
"There are other teachers of the various Hīnayāna schools, such as the Sarvāstivādins, who again offer a defense."
The commentary states:
Regarding my statement that there is a dharma-nature corresponding to all verbal expressions,
it means that first the substance of form exists and is manifested through verbal expression.
Therefore, it is said that [the self] exists;
however, this does not establish the actual nature of the phenomenon.
Thus, we now cite and refute it.
Furthermore, "if various forms reach the point of grasping form" is a restatement of that [opponent's] position.
This implies that although they reach away from form, in reality, [grasping] does not arise.

If the substance of form existed prior to the establishment of the name "form," then even apart from the word "form," one should still give rise to the cognition of "form" regarding that dharma of form.
If the cognition of form were already produced before the name "form" had been established, [it would follow that the cognition is independent of the designation].
What need is there to laboriously establish a name to manifest form?
If the name "form" has not yet been established and the cognition of form has not yet arisen,
it is clear that before the name is known, the substance of form does not exist.
Therefore it is said that, in reality, they do not arise.
Tai (Tài) says:
"It is like a newborn infant who does not yet understand the colors and names of pillars, such as blue, yellow, long, or short."
Therefore, when one perceives a pillar at that time, cognitions such as "blue," "yellow," "long," or "short" do not arise;
it is only subsequently, by relying on the conventional designations of "blue," "yellow," "long," "short," and so forth applied to the pillar, that these cognitions arise.

If it were not established that the name [“pillar”] has not yet been applied, then when one first perceives a pillar, there should arise a cognition of blue, yellow, length, shortness, and so forth regarding the objective entity (rūpa-vastu) of the pillar—the dharmas such as its blue and yellow colors;
however, in reality, such a cognition does not arise.
Therefore, one should know that while the eye-consciousness perceives a pillar, its *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is ineffable.
All that exists apart from phenomena—such as the establishment of blue, yellow, long, short, and so forth—is expressible;
it is the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) that arises in accordance with verbal expression.
The lower fetters are broken; this applies to all categories.
Jing said: Question: [As follows].

When, upon hearing a sound, the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) undergoes conceptualization, its *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) immediately gives rise to an image of the object (*nimitta-bhāga*) termed "form" (*rūpa*).
How can it then be said that phenomena as they are expressed by words lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)?
Furthermore, the mental consciousness takes as its object the conceptualized image of form (*nāma-vikalpa-pratibimba-rūpa*).
Since this image-form is precisely the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
why is it later stated that the dependent nature is the ineffable dharma-nature (*nirabhilāpya-dharmatā*)?
The commentary states:

The color-form that is the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the mental consciousness is in reality a dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), a phenomenon like an illusion or a magical transformation.

When the seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of the mental consciousness perceives and discriminates this image-aspect by means of names, it does not understand it as a causally produced, illusory phenomenon.
Based upon these various delineations upon the dependent nature of form (rūpa), one clings to the existence of a fixed nature;
this self-nature established by the perverted sentiment of clinging to a fixed nature is the thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
Phenomena as expressed by words are ultimately non-existent.
The dependent nature of the image-aspect (nimittabhāga) is not established by the distorted sentiments of verbal expression;
therefore, one cannot say that the image-aspect is the dependent nature.
Various conceptual constructions do not correspond to that dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*);
therefore, the dependent nature remains the ineffable intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
Thus concludes the refutation of the Small Vehicle’s superimpositional attachment.

From here below is the second [section], which refutes the attachment to the deprecatory view of those who, newly entering the Mahāyāna, wrongly grasp at emptiness and thus slander the ineffable intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
This section contains two parts.
At the outset, both individuals are equally ruined and lost within the Buddha-dharma.
Second, the specific characteristics of the ruin and loss of these two individuals are explained.
In the first passage, *vinaya* refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The other two collections are collectively termed "Dharma.
Alternatively, "Dharma" may apply to all three collections;
within these three, that which possesses the sense of discipline and the removal of faults is called Vinaya.
First, regarding those who give rise to the grasping of negation toward phenomena such as form:
this refers back to the previously mentioned grasping at the existence of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature),
which arises in relation to it.
Tai said:
"To reckon that dharmas such as form possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
and to reckon that things such as form possess specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa)."
Second, regarding those who, with respect to the characteristics of conventional designations, give rise to the adherence of negation (*apavāda-grāha*):
this adherence is what is refuted here.
Beiping says:
Regarding the dependent nature as the locus of conventional designation and the perfected nature as the basis for that dependent designation,
the ineffable nature of the dependent and the ultimate reality of the perfected are both utterly non-existent.
Therefore, it is called the "clinging to negation" (*apavāda-grāha*).
Master Ji says:
"The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is termed the 'characteristic of provisional designation' (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*)."
Because it is provisionally designated as having characteristics such as form,
the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is called the "characteristic locus" (lakṣaṇa-sthāna).
Thus, one understands that based upon the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), once the imagined [nature] is removed, there exists true thusness (tathatā).
Thus ends the opening of the two chapters.
From here on, the specific explanation regarding the superimposition of grasping at what is actually non-existent follows; this refers back to the previous refutation.
Regarding the phrase "at the truly existent mere thing" in relation to phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), the second person is explained below.
The text has two parts: first, the direct refutation of the attachment;
second, the citation of scriptural teachings to establish the proof.
Within the former, there are again two sections.
First, the thesis is restated and briefly refuted;
second, the formal refutation is presented following the admission of the opponent's position.
Within the refutation, the argument first employs the combination of dharma, example, and application to provide a decisive critique based on reasoning.
Second, there is a certain class of persons who, regarding those phenomena such as form and so forth, give rise to the adherence to deprecation concerning their existence as mere entities.

This refers to the following: if one holds the view that those phenomena such as form and so forth exist only as mere entities, yet engages in deprecating adherence [regarding their true nature], and so forth.
Jingyun: All phenomena that are conceptually constructed through inverted sentiments and mental fabrications are necessarily delusions regarding reality.
If one relies on the true as being existent or non-existent,
one negates the reality that is the object of delusion;
consequently, the deluded subject— the false— likewise cannot be established as either existent or non-existent.
All of these are unreasonable.
Jñānagarbha says:
"To speak of 'denying the existence' (apavāda-adhyavasāya) refers to the attachment that [the object] is merely a substantial entity (vastu-mātra) within phenomena such as form."
This [position] denies the existence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Jing says:
"The meaning of the analogy is that the provisional is established based on the real; where there is no real, there is no provisional."

To summarize: as for the statement that "in this way, since there are dharmas such as form, and so forth, up to the point that even what is conventionally designated based on a locus must likewise be non-existent," it is like how there must first be a real form (*rūpa*) to be signified before there can be a conventional designation to signify it.
It is not that there is a real unmanifest (avijñapti) while the manifest (vijñapti) is merely conventional;
since the refutation of the manifest has been completed,
we shall next [refute] the basis and that which depends upon it.
If there were only the conventional designation and no underlying reality,
then since there would be nothing for the designation to rest upon, even the designation itself would not exist;
this is precisely what is called the "destruction of all phenomena."
Master Ji said:
"If there is the provisional but no real substance, and since that [substance] does not exist, then the provisional designation should likewise not exist," and so forth.

This means that if one asserts only that there is a provisional designation and the like, which depend upon the dependent nature (paratantra) while lacking the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna), [then the aforementioned fault follows].
The perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is a conventional designation based upon the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
Since there is no basis for dependence, how could there be a conventional designation based on the dependent?
Furthermore, as for this "conventional designation":
This means that while the phenomena that arise exist,
the entities of the dependent and the perfected natures are non-existent.
When universal imagination arises, it necessarily relies upon these two natures.
If there were no basis for the two natures, yet there were a dependent parikalpita (imagined nature), this would be called the destruction of all dharmas.
Ce says: [End of quote].

Regarding the phrase "thus there must be... up to what is expressed by conventional designation," the intended meaning of this interpretation is that there must exist dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which arise from causes and conditions.
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is in reality nothing but the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the thing itself;
only upon this can the conventional designation of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) for phenomena such as form and so forth be established through verbal expression.

It is not the case that without the real existence of the particular characteristic of the dependently arisen thing as a mere entity, there could be the conventional designation of common characteristics through verbal expression.
Second, regarding the person, it refers to the practice as follows:
"There is a certain class of people who, up to and including, give rise to improper and false conceptualizations," etc.
Jing says:
This was said because [the Buddha] wished to refute those among the beginners of the Mahāyāna who have wrongly grasped emptiness; thus he spoke of "a certain class.
When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he taught the doctrine of the Four Noble Truths for the sake of the śrāvakas, so that they might attain the four fruits.
Having attained the four fruits, they transform their attachment to the determinate nature of all existence, realizing that what is truly suffering is indeed suffering, and so forth.
Among them, there are those of indeterminate nature who are capable of turning toward and entering the Mahāyāna.
For these [beings], the Buddha taught the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* in one hundred thousand stanzas to refute the pervasive grasping at [inherent existence].
From the beginning until the negation of the future, he taught exclusively the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Because all practitioners teach in this same manner, it is said that they "teach in common."
The Mahāyāna associated with emptiness is difficult to understand;
therefore, it was not appropriate to teach that the dependent and perfected natures truly exist during the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Consequently, this matter was not mentioned in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*.
Therefore, it is said that they have not yet reached the ultimate, clearly manifest meaning of the profound sūtras of intentional significance;

furthermore, they are unable to understand the intent of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras, which is that only the imaginary nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is purely false and non-existent, while the other two natures are existent.
Relying on the sūtras, they grasp at the general principle that all things are empty;
therefore, it is said that they are unable to understand the meaning of what was taught as it truly is, giving rise to irrational and false conceptualization.
*Ce* (Cemeng) says:
According to the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, there are three wheels of Dharma in the explanation of the text:
first, the wheel of the Four Noble Truths,
such as that found in the four Āgamas and so forth.
Second is the Mahāyāna of signlessness (*animitta*),
which refers to sūtras such as the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* that teach only the signlessness of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Third is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
This refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other texts that fully explain the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Regarding these passages, there are two interpretations in the West.
The Bodhisattva Bhāviveka says:
The various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras are designated as definitive (nītārtha) because they teach that all phenomena are non-apprehendable;
the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra is designated as non-definitive (neyārtha).
Because the three natures are established [in this system] without asserting that all are empty.
Master Dharmapāla said:
"In terms of ultimate reality, there is no distinction between shallow and deep."
However, it is said that fully explaining the three natures constitutes the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*),
whereas failing to do so is non-definitive (*neyārtha*).
As for the statement, "That which is the basis of the conventional, up to and including that which is the ultimate reality," [it refers to this].
Jingyun: All that is false must necessarily rely upon actual reality.
