If actual reality does not exist, the false cannot be established either.
How can you say that all things are merely provisional designations and yet are real?
Ce says: The Master of the Treatise refutes this in turn, stating:
Since you have already negated the dependent nature, that which depends upon it—
the imagined nature— is likewise non-existent. Since the imagined nature does not exist,
[the other two natures do not exist either].
"When will there ever be a perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) that constitutes reality?
This would then be a denial of the two natures.
By this reasoning, [the text] states "there is [nothing] below" and so forth.
Jingyun: You originally slandered the real;
yet since the real has no provisional aspect, to say it does not exist is also called slandering the provisional.
Therefore, it is said that both types constitute slander.
Since their emotional afflictions belong to those [extremes], they are called "utterly non-existent";
once the view of emptiness is established, their practice becomes identical to that of the non-Buddhists.
The *Mahāmaitrī-śāstra* states:
"They cause [others] to be expelled;
they themselves harbor the view of emptiness."
To not expect a future fruit while not planting a present cause is called self-destruction;
it also ruins others who hold the same view.
This concludes the second section, which cites scriptural authority to establish the proof.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, citing the sūtra to provide an explanation;
second, further distinguishing between those who wrongly grasp at emptiness through either evil or wholesome means.
Regarding the preceding section, up to the point where it cites a certain class of those who have wrongly grasped emptiness (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*),
Cè states: "This cites a passage from the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*."
That sutra makes this statement:
"Question: If that is so, why does the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* say that there is no fault for minor [transgressions] but a heavy penalty for major ones?
The explanation says:
Because their respective purposes differ, they do not contradict one another.
The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* is intended to reveal the principle;
since there is no sign (*nimitta*) that contradicts the principle, the transgression is light.
When there is a discrepancy with the principle, the fault is grave;
in the *Akṣayamati-sūtra*, it is for the sake of clarifying practice that there is "conformable practice," and thus the fault is light.
Because views that contradict [right] practice are so grave, why is this?
The following explains the intent of the sutra.
Ce (Cesheng) says:
I see that there is only the fault of deluded objects, and not the six faults.
As for the six faults:
first, there is no fault of slandering the objects of knowledge by asserting that they lack a correct cause.
Second, the fact that one does not fall into the various evil destinies due to this cause clarifies the absence of the fault of evil results.
There are two kinds of self-view:
namely, the conceptualized and the innate.
Because the conceptual view of self is unwholesome, it is able to induce evil results.
In this present passage, the analysis is made based on the innate (sahaja) view for the time being;
this is one interpretation.
However, while it is through the power of others that one may experience rebirth in the evil destinies,
it is not by virtue of this view itself that one falls into the retribution of the evil destinies.
Third, seeking the Dharma from others is the cause for cultivation.
The fourth, "seeking liberation from suffering," refers to seeking the fruit of liberation.
The phrase "not for the sake of falsehood" reiterates that the prior cultivation of causes was not done falsely.
The phrase "not creating delay" reiterates that at the time of realizing the fruit, no obstacles were created.
Fifth, "being able to establish both the teachings and the truths" means being able to establish both the scriptural instructions and the truths they elucidate.
Sixth, "not giving rise to laxity or negligence regarding the various training rules."
Being clear regarding the various points of training (*śikṣāpada*), one does not give rise to indolence.
Second, the detailed analysis of two types of people who grasp at emptiness:
first, the explanation of those who wrongly grasp emptiness (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*).

"Because of that, one does not even believe or accept emptiness" means that one does not believe or accept that the ultimate reality (tattvārtha) is empty by virtue of being the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva),
nor does one believe or accept that it is empty in this regard.
Tai said:
"I do not even accept that the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* exists upon this *paratantra-svabhāva*.
Furthermore, he explained:"

Because the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is absent within this dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it is called "emptiness.
Cè states: "Because the nature of pervasive conceptualization is absent within this dependent nature, it is empty."
Regarding the phrase, "Why? Because that which is empty of it is truly non-existent," Jing says:
This means that because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is deceptive, it is empty; that [imagined nature] is truly non-existent.
Within this ineffable dharmatā, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and so forth are said to be empty because they are devoid of falsity; yet this [emptiness] is truly existent.
By this principle, it can be said that they are empty.
If it is said that even the ineffable intrinsic nature is entirely non-existent,
then the inverted conceptual attachments must have some basis;
upon what basis could they arise?
Therefore, it is said: "Where there is a basis,
there is that which depends upon it and that which is depended upon."
Regarding these two, which one is empty?
Therefore, it is asked: "Which one?
If it is said that both the dependent and the basis are empty, [then...]
The dependent, being false and illusory, can be said to be empty;
but why is the basis, which is true reality, called empty?
Furthermore, one should not say that it is because of this basis that the dependent is false and illusory.
Because that which depends [upon it] is empty, its basis is also said to be empty.
Such attachments as these are precisely what is called "misapprehending emptiness" (*durgṛhītaśūnyatā*). Tái says:
If one says that the three natures are entirely non-existent, then upon what basis would the dependent and perfected natures exist? And how could there be wisdom?
Furthermore, for what reason is the nature of pervasive conceptualization said to be empty?
Another explanation:
what is it in the context of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva),
and by what means is the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) established?
It is empty because of the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Ce (Cesheng) says:
"In what place" refers to the absence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); "of what kind" refers to the absence of the pervasive conceptualized nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
As for the reason for this objection regarding emptiness, Ji says:
"You should not say that it is by virtue of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* [that emptiness is established];
rather, it is within this very context of the *paratantra* and *pariniṣpanna* that [the former] is said to be empty."
Jingyun further uses questions and answers to demonstrate that the two natures are existent.
His questioning is as follows, according to the explanations of the later-day Sanlun masters:
Since all phenomena— whether dependent, thoroughly established, or like that imagined nature— are all false and inverted dharmas whose intrinsic nature is empty,
what fault could there be in saying that this is a "misapprehension of emptiness"?
The commentary states:
That which is grasped through pervasive conceptualization is a distorted mental construction that imagines the existence of a nature that is neither cause nor effect;
it is like a rabbit's horn, whose nature is empty.
Dependence upon others and dependence upon conditions refers precisely to the causes and effects of defilement and purity.
Due to the causal conditions of defilement, one remains for a long time in saṃsāra.
From the arising of pure causes and effects, one reaches the other shore and accomplishes the two bodies of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*.
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is precisely the principle of suchness (*tathatā*).
If one is deluded regarding this principle, one will accumulate [karmic obstructions] for vast aeons.
By realizing this principle, one ultimately emerges from the entanglements to achieve the Buddha-body (dharmakāya).
If these two natures were equally empty as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
they would likewise be non-causal, like the imagined nature itself.
If the dependent nature were not the cause and fruit of defilement,
then sentient beings would have been free from saṃsāra from the very beginning;
if it were not the cause and fruit of purity, there would be no emergence from the mundane state nor the noble paths of the three vehicles.
If you maintain that there are distinctions such as defilement and purification, cause and effect, or ordinary beings and noble ones,
how can you insist that they are identical to the thoroughly imagined nature— which is ultimately non-existent and empty of intrinsic nature?
If you further maintain that from the very beginning there has been no process of saṃsāra and no path for ordinary beings or noble ones to transcend it, then in that case,
the world itself would not exist, nor would there be any slander or faith.
How then can it be said that the teaching of the absence of the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths constitutes slander?
Furthermore, if you maintain that there is neither cause nor effect and all things are empty,
how can there be differences such as those between humans and animals, or between the noble and the lowly?
Since these distinctions are commonly known in the world, they must exist.
Through this examination, one knows that cause and effect within the dependent nature are not non-existent.
Furthermore, if the dependent nature were identical to that imagined nature— being a deceptive phenomenon and ultimately empty—
then the subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) realized by bodhisattvas and others upon emerging from meditative equipoise would be impossible.
Why is it that one relies solely on the causes and effects of the dependent nature for the sake of self-benefit and benefiting others,
while remaining in a state of quiescent cessation without taking the imagined nature as an object?
If both were empty, then one should take both as objects.
Or they may both not be objects of cognition.
Since there is a distinction between that which is an object of cognition and that which is not,
one can know for certain that cause and effect are definitively not empty.
Furthermore, if perfected true suchness (*pariniṣpanna-tathatā*) were also ultimately empty in the same manner as the imagined nature (*parikalpita*),
then the principle of emptiness would be the ultimate reality. Why,
then, would the wisdom of realization (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) not form a conceptualization of emptiness at the moment it correctly realizes and enters [that state]?
Regarding the emptiness of the principle realized, the wisdom that realizes it does not form a conceptual understanding of emptiness;
for such an understanding would contradict the principle.
How, then, can it be called "realization"?

If it is said that this wisdom realizes the principle of emptiness and takes emptiness as its object of understanding, such that the correspondence between subject and object is called "realization," then since it forms an understanding of emptiness, there is conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
How, then, can it be called non-conceptual wisdom realizing the non-conceptual principle of absolute equality? From what could such wisdom arise?
Therefore, True Suchness cannot be said to be empty.
Thus, both the *Śīlasamvara-sūtra* and the old translation of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* state:
"That which is conditioned is called 'the conditioned'."
This refers to the existence of the dependent and the perfected natures.
That which is called "self" and "what belongs to self" is non-existent;
this refers to the emptiness of the imagined nature, which is non-existent.
Although there have been those in the past who were unable to understand this doctrinal point,
it has now emerged through the diligent excavation of the Tripiṭaka.
Thus, treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi* all state that true suchness (*tathatā*) is that which is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness.
By means of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one investigates the two kinds of emptiness;
when fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) arises, it manifests and realizes *tathatā*.
This *tathatā* is not empty.
Furthermore, the old *Saṃdhinirmocana-śāstra* states:
"By means of the three natures, one enters the three non-natures;
therefore, it is known that even the two natures are empty."
This is also untenable. Why?
Because the thoroughly imagined nature is merely a distortion; fundamentally, no such phenomenon exists.
The term "elimination" (*apoha*) is taught in the sense of abandoning inverted mental states;
it is not established based on the dependent or perfected natures, which are non-mental.
How, then, is "elimination" defined?
Question: If it is not eliminated by correct realization, how can there be the "other-dependent" (paratantra), and why is the other-dependent not seen during contemplation?
Explanation:
Thus, within the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), there exists the principle of suchness (tathatā),
as well as the various phenomena of cause and effect;
yet, at the moment of correct entry and realization, one perceives only the suchness of the dependent nature.
One does not perceive dependent phenomena as they truly are;
realized wisdom does not take objective phenomena as its object.
Thus, it is said that words are themselves dispensed with by words.
This is because the two dharmas of phenomena (dharma) and principle (li) always proceed in tandem.
How is this known?
It is just as the two types of wisdom simultaneously contemplate the two truths.

At the very moment that non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) directly realizes suchness (tathatā), subsequent wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) simultaneously takes the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) as its conventional object.

If one were to enter into direct realization [of suchness] exclusively, the dependent nature would necessarily be eliminated; at that same time, subsequent wisdom would consequently lack a conventional object.

If subsequent knowledge, whether simultaneous with or posterior to [non-conceptual knowledge], takes the dependent nature as its object, it may still be termed "dispelling" in relation to non-conceptual knowledge.
If one were to say that subsequent knowledge does not take the imagined nature as its object...
It may be granted that true contemplation dispels the parikalpita (imagined nature),
while subsequent knowledge constantly takes the paratantra (dependent nature) as its object;
why then do you maintain that both are equally dispelled?
Question:
If one clings to the dependent and the perfected as being definitively existent and does not relinquish them,
this definitive clinging to the dependent and the perfected is itself once again a sickness.
What is meant by "the true contemplation of illness does not dispel"?
The explanation states:
it is merely the fabrication of conceptualizations that clings to the existence of two natures.
This concludes the entry into the gate of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

Now, based on the gate of the characteristics of the teachings (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), I shall explain that when the ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpya-svabhāva*) of external objects is realized, it is not discarded.
Such meanings as these cannot be established as identical without relying on the Tripiṭaka.
Now, upon careful examination, this refutation may not necessarily be valid. Why is that?
Now, the Three Treatises (Sanlun) maintain that their fundamental tenet is that meaning has no basis.

How could they permit one to judge that the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) and the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) are identical to the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva)—being uniformly empty and non-existent—and thereby cause an obstacle or difficulty to the doctrine of the Three Treatises?
However, Master Xiao stated that the Three Treatises (Sanlun) exist for the purpose of sweeping away the attachment to views of existence; thus,
they provisionally employ refutation and universal negation to dismantle the nature and meaning of all verbal expressions.
Yoga is for the purpose of dispelling the attachment to a wrongly grasped emptiness; thus, it relies upon the establishment of gateways to extensively present the ineffable dharma.
It provisionally establishes [concepts] without increasing the nature that conforms to words, and provisionally refutes [misconceptions] without diminishing the ineffable dharma.
By this reasoning, there is no contradiction;
these words may be maintained.
Next, the correct apprehension of emptiness is explained.
Jingyun asked:
"Why is it further said that perfect contemplation (*samyak-pratyavekṣā*) is called 'emptiness' (*śūnyatā*)?
It means that because this dependent true dharma-wisdom perceives that which is false and that which does not exist, one contemplates it as empty."
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, by means of this, up to knowing it as it truly is," the terms "this" and "that" refer to each other in mutual relation.
Previously, when the real was contrasted with the false, the real was designated as "this" and the false was named "that."
Now, when we speak of the false in contrast to the true, this is said for the sake of the true;
yet, because these false phenomena are empty, the remaining true phenomena are thereby established as existent.
Therefore, it is said that there is something else truly existent apart from this;
namely, the names that express "form" and so forth with respect to all those entities characterized as form and so on, as previously described.
Regarding the statement that the dharmatā of the conventionally designated phenomena such as form is entirely non-existent:
this means that form and so forth do not exist when constructed according to words.
Therefore, the following section concludes by explaining emptiness.
Regarding the phrase "all these things such as form and their characteristics":
among these, there is the basis for the conventional designation of names such as "form" and so forth.
What, then, is the remainder?
One then identifies that upon which the conventional designation relies as "the other," and that which truly exists outside of the conventional as "the other.
Thus, one knows both of these types exactly as they are— whether real or conventional— without any attachment to increase or decrease.
One does not grasp at the merely conventional nor reject the truly real.
Regarding the statement that "one knows suchness as it is, its nature being beyond words," this refers specifically and preeminently to suchness as having a nature that transcends verbal expression.
The principle that the dependent nature is also ineffable in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—
as T’ai states— is that,
by means of this [dependent nature], the nature of those conceptual constructions is non-existent.
Thus, by means of conceptualization, one correctly contemplates it as empty; furthermore,
because there remains a basis other than this nature of conceptualization— which is the true reality— one knows,
in accordance with reality, that it exists by virtue of that remaining dependent nature.
This is called awakening to and understanding emptiness as it truly is, without error.

Although within this one realizes that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is truly existent, the intention is to clarify that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is empty; that is, emptiness is explained by way of existence.
It speaks only of entering into emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and does not speak of entering into existence (*sattva*).
Kīrti says:
"This means that, by virtue of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), this [nature] is empty of that [imagined nature, *parikalpita-svabhāva*]."
One correctly contemplates it as empty precisely because that which is grasped does not exist;
for when one perceives the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one knows that the grasped object is absent.
Furthermore, by virtue of this very dependent characteristic, the remaining perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) exists.
That is to say, by virtue of the fact that it is other than the pariniṣpanna, one knows it to exist as it truly is;
this means that all those things previously described, such as the conceptual objects of form and so forth, have reached a state of total non-existence.
Subsequently, because that which is grasped as non-existent is further analyzed, it is described as emptiness;
this further analysis analyzes the emptiness of what is grasped by others based upon the dependent nature.
Regarding all such phenomena as the characteristics of form and so forth,
the previous explanation is further questioned to clarify the meaning of "existence" (sat) within the context of the remaining categories;
that is, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) which serves as the basis for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) upon which form and so forth are conventionally designated.
This is a supplement to the [section on] the dependent nature (*paratantra*).

It means that within this [dependent nature], there is what is truly existent as mere phenomena (*vastumātra*), and within those very mere phenomena, there is also what is merely conventional (*prajñaptimātra*).
This is the contemplation of the dependent nature.
One contemplates that the dependent nature consists merely of phenomena which are conventionally existent but not truly existent.
The meaning of the perfected nature as truly existent is clarified below in the treatise.
Cè (Cè) says:
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "it exists as something else," within this dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
there is the principle of being produced by causes and conditions, which is termed "something else.
Because of this "something else," it is known to exist as it truly is.
"Name" refers to the conceptualized objects such as form (*rūpa*) as previously described;
that which is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of the characteristic of form is called "name.
"Object" (*vastu*) refers to the essence (*ātman*).
The substance from which the designation "form" (rūpa) arises is what the old treatise calls the "delimitation of phenomena" (vastu-paryanta).

As for the statement that the dharmas of the nature of conventional designations, such as form and so forth, are entirely non-existent: this refers to the fact that the objects designated by names like "form" have no intrinsic reality whatsoever.
These forms and so forth, which are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*), lack any real nature.
The *Old Treatise* states that they are "delimitations of provisional designations" (*prajñapti-vyavasthāna*).
To say that both of these types are known as they truly are means:
Knowing emptiness and knowing existence.
Second, regarding the citation of scriptural authority for the proof, the text is divided into three parts.
First is the general enumeration.
Next, the scripture is cited for explanation,
followed by a concluding summary after the explanation is complete.

The original term is *ārya*,

*Āgama* here means "teaching."
*Āgama* means "words that have arrived.

it should not be called the "Holy Teaching" (*āgama*).
There are three parts to the scriptural citation used for the explanation.
Regarding the initial citation of the *Bhavasaṃkrānti-sūtra*,

That sutra clarifies that because the four modes of existence—namely, death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*), intermediate existence (*antarā-bhava*), and so forth—circulate in an indeterminate manner, they are called "transmigrating existences" (*vartamāna-bhava*). Jī says:
There is this adherence to existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*),
namely, the reckoning that the essence of what is expressed by names corresponds to those names.
Apart from this, there is the reckoning of "existence" which is called the *parivarta-sūtra*.
The commentary on the verse states:
"The first half clarifies that the nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva), which follows verbal expression, is entirely non-existent.
The second half clarifies that the dependent (paratantra) and the perfected (pariniṣpanna) lack that nature of following verbal expression."
This is the ineffable intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The intention is to take the latter part as the explanation.
Ce (Cemoti) says:
The first half clarifies that, based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there are the provisional designations of the means of realization and the object of realization.
The third line clarifies that within the dependent nature, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist.
The fourth line clarifies that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) exists.
In the Master’s commentary, it says:
"That is to say, regarding the conceptualization of phenomena such as form, up to describing them as nirvāṇa. Tái says:
This passage explains the preceding two lines.
One establishes the name "imaginary nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) for phenomena that are the objects of perceptions such as "form";
one then expresses and describes those phenomena which are the objects of perceptions such as "form" by means of these very names, "imaginary nature," and so forth.
Some say it is form (*rūpa*), and so on, up to saying it is nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, another explanation states that "perception" (*saṃjñā*) is a name (*nāman*).
This means that upon those phenomena designated by names such as "form" and so forth, one establishes the conventional designations (prajñapti) of "form" and so forth;
it is precisely by means of these conventional designations of phenomena such as form that one expresses and speaks of the phenomena designated by names such as "form."
Ce says: The old treatise states that one explains all phenomena as empty by means of names such as "form" and so forth.
The circulating teachings speak of form (*rūpa*) up to and including *nirvāṇa*.
According to this text, one knows that the first half-verse concerns the teaching on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Within all these conceptualized phenomena of form and so forth, the nature of form and so forth is entirely non-existent.
Jingyun said:
Within these phenomena (dharma) which are names capable of designating all these forms, the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of form and so forth is entirely non-existent;
furthermore, the referent (artha) signified by the name "form" and so forth does not exist, nor does there exist any other form or the like that is to be designated.
Therefore, it is said that while there are no other phenomena such as form and so forth,
the ineffable nature of reality truly exists within the basis upon which the names and phenomena of form and so forth— which are conceptually constructed— depend.
Tài says: This explains the following two lines.
This refers to the nature of discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva) designated by all these conventional names such as "form" and so forth.
According to the Sarvāstivādins, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and so forth is entirely non-existent.
This is like the Sāṃkhyas positing the three qualities (*guṇa*)—sorrow, joy, and darkness—as the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
or like the Vaiśeṣikas positing the fourth category (*padārtha*), "existence" (*sattā*), and the sixth category, "inherence" (*samavāya*).
This is the intrinsic nature of form and so forth, yet it is not form and so forth.
To clarify that these two [views] held by non-Buddhists do not exist, it is said that there is also no other intrinsic nature of form and so forth;
however, within that nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), [it exists].
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is the basis upon which the various conceptual natures designated by conventional terms such as "form" (*rūpa*) rely,
possesses a true reality that is the ineffable nature of meaning;
one should know that this is precisely the intrinsic nature of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Ce says: This means that within these phenomena of form and so forth belonging to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there is no such self-nature (*svabhāva*) of form and so forth as is imagined by the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
Regarding the statement "nor is there any other nature of form and so forth," there are two interpretations.
One version states:
Master Yuan says that they are called "other dharmas" because they exist in contrast to those [primary ones].
It is not the case that because [certain things] are definitely non-existent, it can be said that other dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth also lack intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*).
This explanation is incorrect.
As the old treatise states:
The dharmas such as form likewise lack any other intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
For this reason, the explanation is made thus.
Now, according to the New Treatise (Abhidharmakośa-śāstra), it says:
Furthermore, there are no other dharmas with the nature of form and so forth.
Therefore, one should know that "the remainder" does not refer to the non-existence of form.
Now, let us explain this interpretation.
Regarding the previous statement, "Nor is there a self-nature apart from those [phenomena] that is the range of speech or the domain of speech," there are two interpretations.
One says:
Having refuted each and every alternative position—that there exists a distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva) external to that which is dependent upon others—he says:

"In our school, although phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are conventionally established, there exists a nature of form and so forth that is distinct from form and the like; this is precisely the fourth category among the six categories (*ṣat-padārtha*), namely the category of 'substance' (*dravya*)."
Therefore, it is universally refuted as follows:
there are no other phenomena such as form (rūpa) or other natures;
yet, within that dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) truly exists.
Jizang says:
This means that upon the dharmas of form as conceived by the parikalpita (imagined), there is no such intrinsic nature as the form and so forth grasped by the parikalpita;
it is not merely that the intrinsic nature grasped as form and so forth is absent.
Furthermore, within the nature of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*), there is no other nature of form-dharmas such as fragrance, odor, and so forth.
Regarding the second meaning of the *Sūtra*,
Master Jing says:
Regarding the phrase "such as the *Anantārthasūtra* and others," it refers to the *Arthavargīya*.
Jñānagarbha states:
"It is the *Arthavargīya* of the *Abhidharmasūtra*."
Cè (Ce) says:
This is the title of one chapter from the *Zhuan you jing* (Sūtra on Turning Existence).
It consists of four lines of verse.
The intent is to grasp that which is neither grasped nor not grasped, and neither craved nor not craved, thereby realizing the ineffable intrinsic nature.
Ce (Ceci) comments:
"In the first three lines, the objective sphere is presented in relation to the person; by showing non-attachment toward phenomena, the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is manifested."
The final phrase directly establishes the supreme benefit.
As the long passage states: "That which is called the objects of perception such as worldly forms, up to the Sage who is unattached."
Tai said:
"The World-Honored One, the Muni, does not cling to any worldly conventional conceptual natures.
Since he does not cling, [he is free from attachment]."
Who could grasp at or conceptualize dharmas of the nature of discrimination?
Because there is no attachment, what is seen or heard does not give rise to craving.
This refers to the objects of the nature of discrimination designated by conventional names, such as "form" and so forth, within the world.
The nature of discrimination, which is the referent of various conventional designations such as "form" and so forth, is called the "conventional.

Because one perceives the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva), which is clung to according to its names upon the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), as being free from the views of increase or decrease,

Tai says:
The passage from "For what reason? up to "not clinging to things through the superimposition or denial [of their existence]" explains the third phrase.
The seeds of the two extreme views are called the "view of superimposition and denial," while the manifestation of these two extremes is called "present perversion."
Because the Muni possesses the vision of seeds that are free from the two extremes,
and because he has no manifesting inverted views,
the Muni is, by this principle, called "unattached."
Thus, for one who is free from attachment,
who else could grasp at the nature of discrimination?
This is because they have abandoned the views based on the seeds of the two extremes.
Regarding the reality of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one does not grasp at the two extremes.
From "regarding the objects of knowledge" up to "therefore it is called non-attachment," this explains the fourth line.
Because the Muni is able to correctly contemplate the objects of knowledge—the reality of the dependent nature—he is said to possess "vision."
Furthermore, because the three types of persons beyond training (aśaikṣa) are collectively termed "Sages" (muni),
and because a Sage hears from others the verbal expressions concerning the objects of knowledge— the reality that depends upon others— he is called "one who has heard" (śruta).
Because one does not cling to the objects of these sights and sounds,
craving does not arise initially, nor does it increase once it has arisen;
one realizes only the dependent reality of the object-condition.
Therefore, one ultimately severs attachment, craving, and grasping, abiding always in supreme equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The third section of the text is divided into two parts;

The latter part explains the meaning of the sūtra.
The former part consists of three sections;
first is a brief exposition.
Next is the re-explanation.

Cè stated:
"This is a follower of the Mahāyāna, not the Śrāvaka-vehicle Kātyāyana."
The World-Honored One spoke thus to him:
"One does not rely on the four great elements or the four formless realms,

Nor does one rely on the orbs of the sun and moon to grasp the signs of light;
nor does one rely on what is seen, heard, sensed, or known through skillful means to seek that which is rightly intended;
nor does one rely on mental consciousness.
Although one investigates through vitarka and vicāra, one does not practice dhyāna by relying on any nature of conceptual construction;
the intended meaning here is that one practices dhyāna by relying solely on the dependent true nature (paratantra-satya).
Zhongbian says:
"Regarding the phrase 'or eliminating the perception of earth with respect to earth,' Jing says:"

"It means that regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), when one can correctly eliminate the two extremes of superimposition and denial through the conventional designation of 'earth' and so forth, this is termed 'elimination'."
Third, regarding the clarification of the benefits of contemplation:
"Indra" refers here to Śakra;

The *Jiaojielun* (Treatise on the Explanation of Terms) states that Śakra-devendra and the Brahmās of both the Great and Small [Heavens] all come to pay homage and respect.
As for the phrase "those who do not know" mentioned in the verse:
"Practicing dhyāna while detached from signs transcends the realms of the heavens;
it is said so because those [heavenly beings] cannot reach it.
Below, the Master of the Treatise explains the intent of the sutra.
Without yet explaining this verse,
he instead explains the prose passage cited immediately prior, which mentions "removing the perception of earth" and so forth.
The meaning of these [passages] is as follows:
Regarding the objects apprehended through the conceptualization of "earth" and so forth across all stages:
from this conceptualization of "earth," one provisionally designates them by the name "earth" and so forth;
thus, these are called "conceptualizations arising from conceptualization."
Name is also called conceptualization; it is termed "investigation" and "conceptualization.
Regarding those entities such as form that are spoken of, there must necessarily be superimposition or negation.

He eliminates, severs, and abandons that perception.
The third [section] clarifies the intention for its exposition:
as stated above, all phenomena are beyond verbal expression.
For what reason do the Buddhas give rise to verbal expression regarding the ineffable Dharma?
If the teaching accords with the Dharma, the Dharma is not ineffable;
if the teaching contradicts the Dharma, it is of no benefit.
The answer is fourfold:
first, being unable to explain it to others;
second, explaining it but others not hearing it.
Third, because others do not hear it and do not know it;
fourth, because the Buddhas speak so that others may hear and come to know it.
This is the intended meaning.
Although the Dharma is beyond words,
in order to cause others to understand this wordless Dharma,
it is explained through skillful means by means of provisional names and signs.
If one does not give rise to speech, others will not hear or know that single dharma which transcends words.
Therefore, for the sake of benefiting others, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas employ provisional names and conceptual designations within the nameless;
this is to manifest the wordless by means of words.
As it is said in the *Viniścaya*:
"Question: If it is said that all phenomena are ineffable, does this statement not itself refer to the phenomena that are spoken of?"
If they were congruent, then all phenomena would be expressible.
If they are not congruent, how can one say that phenomena are inexpressible?
The answer is:
Since my own established thesis is likewise refuted by that [opponent], this fault does not apply.
My established thesis is the statement that all phenomena are inexpressible; this very statement is also what I have established.
Furthermore, because this is also refuted, there is no such fault.
From here on, the fourth section clarifies how ordinary fools, failing to understand the teaching that transcends words, give rise to the eight types of conceptualization.
This contains four parts.
First, it clarifies that through non-comprehension, eight types of conceptualization arise.

Second, it explains that for the sake of understanding the faults of conceptualization, one cultivates the four investigations (*vitarka*) and four analyses (*vicāra*), as well as the four kinds of knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

Third, regarding these four kinds of knowledge of reality, it clarifies how ordinary beings, due to their ignorance, give rise to conceptualization and thus undergo an uninterrupted cycle of transmigration.

Fourth, based on these four types of knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), the following clarifies how the Bodhisattva, by means of wisdom, understands and distinguishes [reality], thereby able to realize the great fruit.
In the first [section] there are three parts.

First, it clarifies that because one does not understand that all phenomena are beyond words, eight types of conceptualization arise, which give rise to the three entities and, in turn, can produce the two worlds.
Next, the eight kinds of discrimination are explained.
Following this, the mutual production of the first three types of discrimination among these eight with their respective bases and objects is analyzed.
Within the former [section], there are three parts.
First, a general presentation;
second, a detailed explanation;
third, a discernment of the phenomena produced, including their origins and manifestations, which encompasses the dharma exhaustively.
The initial passage merely clarifies that the failure to realize *tathatā* gives rise to the eight types of conceptualization;
it does not briefly explain how the failure to realize the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is beyond verbal expression, gives rise to the eight types of conceptualization.
Among the three matters that arise, the first concerns the basis of conditions:
the supported is the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*),
and the supported object is the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
The latter two matters both concern sentient beings.
In the second section, the detailed explanation, the text is divided into three parts.
First, the distinct names are enumerated.
Next, the three things that can produce [the eight types of discrimination] are distinguished.
Finally, these are summarized into three things, briefly explained through three gates to distinguish the eight types of discrimination.
First, their names are listed and their essential natures are identified.
The names are listed as in the text. Regarding the identification of their essential nature (*svabhāva*),
Jing recounts the words of the Tripiṭaka Master:
Furthermore, it takes as its object the fundamental grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and grasping at a person (*pudgalagrāha*) that are about to arise.
The preparatory mental states (*prayoga-citta*) for these graspings—such as attachment, aversion, and delusion regarding a person—have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature;
thus, their nature is not defiled (*asaṃkliṣṭa*).
That is to say, within that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*), there is the non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) wisdom that is not skillful;

from this, the fundamental dual grasping at self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*) and the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion arise through conceptualization—this is what constitutes defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
How is this known?
The subsequent passage states:
"It is because of such false conceptualization that various defilements arise."
Because of various defilements (*saṃkleśa*), one transmigrates through birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
This passage refers to the eight kinds of conceptualization (*vikalpa*);
however, because it is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) and not a defilement, [it does not lead to transmigration].
Although fundamental attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is not defiled when viewed from the perspective of those two vehicles,
it is indeed defiled when viewed from the perspective of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, the fundamental [afflictions] produced by the eight types of conceptual discrimination are all termed "defiled."
When the three types of discrimination first arise and the fundamental threefold grasping at phenomena occurs,

they take as their objects the self-supporting body and the vessel-world, and by means of the perceived aspects (nimitta-bhāga) thus reached, they perfume and establish the seeds of the self-body and the vessel-world.
After being born there, one's own body and the external vessel-world arise;
one's own body is called the "basis," while the external vessel is called the "condition."
Once they have arisen based on conditions, they immediately give rise to the three fundamental types of attachment to dharmas.

Next, the two [subsequent] conceptualizations serve directly as the means by which they can give rise to the fundamental attachments to self and what belongs to the self, as well as to the conceit of "I am."
Regardless of whether the subsequent views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth arise from perfumed seeds,
the latter three types of discrimination universally serve as the preliminary means (*upāya*) that draw forth the fundamental greed, hatred, and delusion;
nor does it matter whether greed and so forth arise only after seeds have been perfumed.
It may also be said that the first three types of discrimination are precisely the fundamental grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
This occurs because, by taking the self-body and the vessel-world as objects, the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) perfumes its own seeds within the seeing-part.
After the seeds have been perfumed by the image-aspect (nimittabhāga),
they take the self-body and the vessel-world as their supporting conditions (ālambana-pratyaya).
Once these supporting conditions have arisen, they in turn produce the substance of the threefold simultaneous conceptualization consisting of dharma-grasping (dharmagrāha).
Therefore, the text below states:
"That is to say, past conceptualization, acting as a cause, is able to produce present conceptualization which serves as its basis and condition;
once this present basis and condition have arisen, it in turn can act as a cause to produce [conceptualization] in the present."
Due to that discrimination arising from its objective conditions,
the subsequent two types of discrimination constitute the fundamental seeds of the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), which have been perfumed;
these in turn give rise to the subsequently produced views of self and what belongs to the self, as well as the other four views and the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*), serving as their foundation.
When this [consciousness] takes "I" and "mine" as its objective conditions (*ālambana*), it should likewise infuse seeds that give rise to subsequent bases and conditions;
the text briefly clarifies the arising of its own specific fruit (*svabhāga-phala*),
but does not analyze the matter of the bases and conditions for the arising of the views of "I" and "mine."
The subsequent three types of discrimination are the very essence of fundamental greed, hatred, and delusion; upon arising,
they immediately perfume and establish seeds of their own kind,
which subsequently give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion at a later time.
When greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth arise through conditions and bases, they should likewise infuse seeds that give rise to all subsequent conditions and bases;
furthermore, this has been stated briefly.
Beipin says:
Generally, the first three types of discrimination are identified as the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and its preparatory stages (*pūrvaprayoga*).
Among these three types of discrimination, it is the "reckoning" (*vikalpa*) that is meant here,
because it functions by taking the twelve bases— the sense organs, their objects, and the consciousnesses— as its objective conditions.
The first [type of discrimination] has the nature of the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) based on the fundamental means (*upāya*).
The next two have the nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) regarding the means for grasping at a self (*pudgala-grāha*).
The final three have the nature of conceptualization regarding both types of grasping (*grāha*) and the means for those two graspings.
Taiyun said:
"The first three [aspects of] discrimination take the grasping of dharmas as their essence;
the latter two discriminations merely give rise to views and pride."
Because it is a preliminary preparation:
following the conceptualization of "I" and "mine," the subsequent existence of "I" and "mine" is then termed the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Due to this view of self, the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*) subsequently arises.

From the two types of discrimination, views and pride arise; of these, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) serves as the basis for the arising of the remaining four views, while the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) serves as the basis for the arising of the seven types of pride and so forth.
The final three types of discrimination are the skillful means (*upāya*) for the three poisons.
Master Ji said:
"The first three are skillful means for the grasping at dharmas;
the fourth and fifth are skillful means for the grasping at persons."
The latter three are skillful means for the three poisons;
furthermore, the first three are skillful means for the two types of grasping,
while the fourth and fifth are exclusively skillful means for the grasping of a person.
These eight types of discrimination do not all involve the grasping of dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
This is because when the grasping of a person (*pudgalagrāha*) and so forth arise, the grasping of dharmas does not induce karmic retribution.
Since it is stated that they can produce the three factors, [the grasping of dharmas must be included].
Therefore, it is known that the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and so forth serve as the means.
If that is so, since the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) also pervades the unwholesome nature, why is it not included?
If one does not grasp at the indeterminate view of self,
one grasps at other unwholesome ones;
as for the latter three, one does not grasp at their roots.
This briefly distinguishes between that which produces [the poisons] as a means (*upāya*) and that which is produced from the root.
It clarifies that the latter three serve as the means capable of producing the three root poisons.
Therefore, it also adopts the provisional means (*upāya*).
If these are correlated with the seven types of differentiation,
