Regarding the general designation as "discrimination" (vikalpa):
In the Sanskrit original, it is called *vikalpa*,
which here means "discriminating consciousness.
That which possesses the three types of reflection is [the mind].
The original term is *saṃkalpa*, which means "volition" (*cetanā*).
It should not be categorized as one of the three types of discrimination (*vikalpa*).
The original term is samyaksaṃkalpa; this is translated as "right intention" (正思惟).
It is a designation within the Eightfold Noble Path.
The old treatise states that the eight deluded conceptions do not correspond to the Sanskrit original;
therefore, the term "discrimination" (fenbie) is retained.
"Eight" is merely a numerical designation.
Thus, names are established based on their numerical count and their underlying meaning. Regarding the specific names:
although there are eight names, they receive three designations.
First, the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), which is threefold: pleasant, unpleasant, and neutral.
These five types of conceptualization are named according to their objects.
Because it conceptualizes the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, it is called "conceptualization of intrinsic nature."
It is called "discrimination of distinctions" because it discriminates the various differences within the objects of the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, there are three kinds of objective referents (*ālambana*):
those that accord with one's mind are called "desirable" (*iṣṭa*).
That which contradicts the object and opposes the mind is called "unpleasant" (*aniṣṭa*).
That which opposes both [object and mind] regarding neutral objects is called "contradictory" (*ubhayaviparīta*).
The two types of grasping through conceptualization are named after their respective objects and modes of grasping.
"Always" and "many phenomena" refer to the object of grasping.
"Grasping" is the name for the fault of the subject that grasps.
The three types—self, what belongs to self, and conceptualization—derive their names from the mode of cognitive engagement (*vijñapti*).
The nature of objects is neither self nor what belongs to a self, yet one forms the conception of them as self and what belongs to a self.
The third pair clarifies the inclusion of the five stages of abiding (pañca-vāsabhūmi).
As for these five stages of abiding:
First, the stage of abiding in the view of one place;
second, the stage of abiding in the craving for desire;
third, the stage of abiding in the craving for form.
The four bases of attachment to the formless realm and the fifth,
the basis of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*).
The former three are subsumed within the basis of the abiding of discerning ignorance.
Regarding the two types of discrimination between "self" and "what belongs to self," there are two kinds.
If it is conceptually arisen (*vikalpita*), it is subsumed under the ground of abiding in a single locus (*ekadeśasthiti-bhūmi*).
If it is innate (*sahaja*) self-view, it pervades all three grounds and is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding the subsequent three types of discrimination, the discrimination of the unloved is subsumed solely within the craving for sensual desire (*kāmatṛṣṇā*).
The remaining two types of discrimination pertain to all three bases of craving (*tṛṣṇā-sthāna*).

This section, for the time being, explains their mutual inclusion according to the interpretation of the Master [Vasubandhu], who takes the two types of grasping (*upādāna*) and so forth as the essence of the eight types of discrimination.
This does not define the meaning of "teacher" as having the nature of wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate through the application of skillful means.
As the text states: "These three kinds of discrimination can produce the objective bases and conditions upon which conceptual proliferation depends."
Jingyun: Discursive proliferation (*prapañca*) is the mind that takes objects as its conditions;
"relying on conditions" refers to what the mind depends upon.
The statement "that which is called the ideation of form and so forth" refers to the designating name (*nāman*), which is the basis for verbal expression.
"Serving as the objective condition" refers to the designated object (*vastu*).
The phrase "subsumed under discourse" further clarifies the designating name.
Regarding "that which is manifested by names, concepts, and verbal expressions":
this further clarifies the activities of the signified object.
This name and its referent constitute the conceptualized object of discrimination and the proliferation of discursive elaboration (*prapañca*).
"That which discriminates and calculates this very object into numerous and manifold categories" refers to the arising of the faculty of discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Tai [Sheng] says:

Regarding the statement that the mind which grasps through pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita) is called "discriminative proliferation" (vikalpa-prapañca) because it has a basis (āśraya) and an object (ālambana),
there are three explanations from the West.
The first says:
The basis for discrimination consists of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
The conceptualization of pervasive attachment consists of the seven consciousnesses and the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
That which arises simultaneously with the sixth mental consciousness is that which arises together with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
Although it does not directly rely upon the five sense faculties,
because it is inseparable from the five consciousnesses, the five faculties are also said to be its supports.
Following the simultaneous discernment by the five consciousnesses, a subsequent mental consciousness arises to conceptually evaluate the five sensory objects.
Therefore, it is also said that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes the five sense organs as its successive supports.
Consequently, the mental consciousness is said to have all six organs as its bases.
That the objects of perception (ālambana) are the six sense-fields (ṣaḍviṣaya) is easily understood.
The second explanation states:
that which is the basis is one's own five-aggregate body;
that which is the object of focus consists of the bodies of others and the receptacle world.
The third explanation states:
that which is the basis is the meaning (artha),
and that which is the object of cognition is the name (nāman).
In this region, there was previously this commentary on the *Treatise on the Three Non-natures*:
"Regarding the perception of the aggregate of form and the other four aggregates up to nirvāṇa, as well as the things designated by names such as 'form'—
these are called the referents."
One discriminates by means of names and meanings.
Based on names, conceptualizing thoughts arise and verbal expressions are produced.
Because names, conceptions, and verbal expressions serve as causes, discrimination arises.
Because conceptualization is comprised of and manifested by names, notions, and verbal expressions, it is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
As for why only these three types of conceptualization are said to produce their respective bases and objects: [it is because they are the primary causes].
Due to this discrimination, which is the conceptualization of grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*),
when seeds are perfumed by all categories [of experience],

the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world arise from these three types of discriminative seeds; for they constitute the support and the object-condition (*ālambana*) for the myriad things.
The latter five types of discrimination are the afflictions of skin and flesh; based on these three factors, grasping arises.
Therefore, they cannot directly reach the many categories of the support and the object.
Master Ji said:
"That which is said to be 'comprised' refers to being comprised within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
furthermore, that which is 'comprised' also extends to untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*)."
Now it is further explained:
what was previously called "outflow-free" (anāsrava) is not produced by the three types of discrimination;
that which is produced is something else.
That which is "encompassed" refers to its retinue;
that which is "manifested" refers to phenomena such as the sense faculties and their objects, as these are what are manifested. Cè says:
Question: Since the various faculties, such as the eye, all arise from the perfuming of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect),
and it is this [aspect] that constitutes discrimination (*vikalpa*),
why is it stated here that the threefold discrimination is the producer?
The commentary states:
According to the actual reality,
the seeds of the image-aspect (nimittabhāga) are able to produce the sense organs, such as the eye, as well as their objects.
Regarding the statement that "the three parts are capable of producing":
the perfuming of the *nimittabhāga* (image-part) must depend upon the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part) before it can be perfumed;
it is with reference to this predominant function that they are said to be "capable of producing."
The matters produced by the subsequent two and the following three are as stated in the text.
Regarding the second section, the detailed explanation of the eight kinds of discrimination, there are seven sentences;
each sentence is individually analyzed, explained, and concluded.
Jingyun: Regarding the two explanations for the essence of discrimination, they are as previously stated;
for now, I shall explain according to the latter interpretation.
Regarding the explanation of the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*),
it says: "That which pertains to all things conceived as form and so forth" refers to the referents of names such as "form" and so on.
"Distinguishing the various intrinsic natures of form and so forth" means that,
based on names such as "form," one distinguishes the intrinsic nature of form and so forth that corresponds to those names.
Regarding the phrase "all conceptual investigations":
The substance of the capacity for discernment emerges;
this is consistent with what is stated in this treatise.
From the second dhyāna upward, there is no vitarka or vicāra.
How can the higher stages possess the substantial nature of vitarka (investigation) and vicāra (analysis)?
The explanation says:
vitarka and vicāra are merely provisional designations.
Its intrinsic nature consists of either volition or wisdom.
If judged by its function, it exists only in the lower stages;
if judged by its substantial entity, it extends to the higher stages as well.
Therefore, the eight types of discrimination pervade all stages.
Furthermore, the *Bhūmi-vibhāga* states:
"If one considers the discrimination of vitarka and vicāra in relation to supramundane, untainted, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)," [it is not found therein].
According to this text, all mental phenomena within the three realms are conceptualizations (*vikalpa*).
Based on this statement,
there are both general and specific types of discursive investigation and conceptualization.
The specific names "vitarka" (applied thought) and "vicāra" (sustained thought) exist only in the lower stages;
the general term "vitarka-vicāra" exists in the higher stages as well.
This is explained in the *Vibhaṅga*.
That is to say, regarding this which possesses form:
if one discriminates and grasps at the existence of form as being the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), that is an exaggeration (*samāropa*).
If one discriminates the existence of form as being the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), that is not an exaggeration.
This means that this formlessness also has two aspects:
if one discriminates by saying that imagined form is non-existent, that is correct;
if one discriminates by saying that dependent form is non-existent, that is erroneous.
The categories such as "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) and "without resistance" (*apratigha*) are to be understood through classification.
That is to say, that which is "visible" (*sanidarśana*) refers to the objective field of form (*rūpa-āyatana*), which is capable of being seen.
Other particles and sense organs cannot produce visual perception;
therefore, they are called "non-visible.
This differs from the explanation given in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
To have the capacity for cognitive discernment is what constitutes a "gate.
Tai says:
To speak of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) as having a substantial entity is itself an intrinsic discrimination (svabhāva-vikalpa).
The differentiation of names according to various categories is called "differentiation by designation.
Regarding the term "visible," the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* and other texts refer to it as "visible" (*sanidarśana*) or "invisible" (*anidarśana*).
According to the correct translation based on the Sanskrit manuscript, it is named "with-vision" (*savipaśyanā*) and "without-vision" (*avipaśyanā*).
The *Xianyang lun* (Śrāvakabhūmi), in its third section on discrimination (*viniścaya*), explains these as "vitarka" and "vicāra.
In this treatise, within the context of the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), it refers specifically to "all vitarkas."
One should know that while the eight types of discrimination are explained here in their specific application, taken collectively they have the single number as their essence.
Furthermore, regarding their general definition of essence,
one should know that they have the mind and mental factors of the three realms as their essence.
Among the three types of discrimination, intrinsic discrimination (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) extends only up to the first dhyāna,
because from the second dhyāna upward, there is wisdom characterized by manifest discernment (*saṃprakhyāna-bhāgīya-prajñā*).
As for the discrimination of grasping as a whole (*piṇḍa-grāha-vikalpa*):
Tai said:
"It is like forming an army from chariots, infantry, elephants, and horses,
or forming a forest from many trees."
The formation of food, drink, and so forth from the four sense-objects consists entirely of composite phenomena (*saṃghāta-dharma*),
because one clings to the notion that these four sense-objects possess a fixed, inherent nature.

Furthermore, there is the conceptualization of grasping at the totality (*piṇḍagrāha-vikalpa*), which arises from grasping at the existence of a determinate, conventional dharma that is a composite of the four sense-objects, such as food and drink;
because one grasps at this collective phenomenon, it is called the conceptualization of grasping at the totality.
If one reckons that the five aggregates possess a substantial reality...

To conceptually construct a "person," "self," "sentient being," and so forth, based on the five aggregates of these sentient beings as a mere designation, is called the "discrimination of grasping at the whole.
Even up to the stage of an Arhat, this discrimination remains; it is a mental affliction and a skillful means [of the afflictions].

Jingyun: This general grasping at the conceptual construction of "self" and "sentient beings," which is induced by provisional designations, is no different from the subsequent conceptualization of "I" and "mine. What distinction could there possibly be between them?
The commentary states:
The present mention of "self," "sentient beings," and so forth does not rely upon the grasping at a substantial self or sentient beings as existing entities.
Now, taking as an example what is conventionally designated and commonly known in the world as "I," "sentient being," or "living soul"—
this is grasped by taking the phenomena of the five aggregates and so forth collectively; therefore, this is a form of grasping,
not the grasping of a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*).
Master Ji says:
"The 'grasping at a totality' refers to the two types of grasping;
the distinction between the 'grasping at a self' and the 'grasping at what belongs to a self' exists only in relation to persons."
Regarding the phrase "the conceptualization of 'I' and 'mine' (*ātma-ātmīya-vikalpa*) and so forth," Jing says:
This means that if various phenomena (*vastu*) are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and with grasping (*sopādāna*), they emerge as the objects of the calculation of "mine" (*mama-kāra*).
These are precisely the five appropriated aggregates of outflows.
Within these aggregates of appropriation, one has long practiced the grasping of "I" and "mine," and over a great length of time,
such a view of self has accumulated.
Regarding the statement that "false discrimination arises conditioned by objects within one's own sphere of views due to the habitual practice of those false attachments in previous lives":
this refers to the habitual practice regarding those appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*) in previous lives.
Based on the objects within one's own field of perception, the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*) repeatedly arises.
Subsequently, among the three types of discrimination, craving arises toward pure objects and aversion arises toward impure ones;
furthermore, delusion (*moha*) and other afflictions arise in relation to both pure and impure objects, as well as neutral objects that are neither.
The meaning of the textual passage is clear. T'ai states:
"The conceptualization of 'I' and 'mine' arises only in ordinary persons, because it originates from conditions related to the contaminated aggregates of self and others."
Regarding all contaminated phenomena and the aggregates,
due to long-standing habituation since beginningless time, one gives rise to the conceptualization of "I" and "mine";
yet, this is not yet a definitive grasping that these are "I" or "mine."
Following this conceptualization, the dogmatic adherence of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) subsequently arises;
following the view of self, pride (*māna*) is then produced.
Furthermore, it is due to the mind of deliberative conceptualization that one perceives objects as being discordant, concordant, or neutral.
From this discriminating mind, greed, hatred, and delusion subsequently arise.
Cè (Cé) says:
"The terms 'with outflows' (sāsrava) and 'with grasping' (sopādāna) [refer to this]."
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, "outflow" (āsrava) is explained through three meanings:
that which arises from outflows,
and that which is capable of producing outflows.
Because they are the locus of outflows (*āsrava*),
they are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
Now, the Mahāyāna explains "outflow" through six meanings.
This refers to their nature as outflows (*āsrava*),
and so on, up to their being of a heavy class;
the full explanation is as given in the *Abhidharma-śāstra*.
These very outflows (āsrava) that possess the four kinds of grasping (upādāna) are called "with-grasping" (sopādāna).
Third, regarding the explanation of the eight [factors], the first three clarify how they mutually produce one another with their respective bases and objects.
Jingyun: Within the past body, three types of discrimination arise,
which perfume and form the seeds of the self-body that serves as the basis, as well as the seeds of the objective world of the vessel.
It is able to produce all the bases and conditions existing in the present life;
because one does not clearly understand these present bases and conditions,
conceptualization arises when they occur.
Subsequently, based on that objective condition-seed, there arises at a future time that objective basis which is its support;
when it is about to arise in the future, based on that objective condition,
it will certainly arise as a support for the subsequent discrimination.
Tài says: Although "discrimination" (vikalpa) is mentioned here in a general sense,
among the first three dharmas, discrimination is the fundamental one.
However, regarding the first three types of discrimination, they arise in mutual dependence upon their respective bases, names, meanings, and objects;
whereas for the latter five types of discrimination, there is no separate entity for the object,
nor do they extend to names and meanings.
Therefore, it is not explained separately.

From here on, the second section clarifies the cultivation of the four investigations and the four kinds of knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) for the purpose of thoroughly understanding the faults of the eight types of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
This section contains two parts.
The first part consists of a question and answer that provides a general summary;
the latter part provides a detailed enumeration.
Question: By reason of the mutual relationship between understanding and delusion, it follows logically that their causes and conditions should be identical.
Why is it that while delusion takes true reality as its object, the mind of liberation takes conceptual discrimination as its object?
The explanation says:
regarding the universal meaning of reality, both are equal; prior to this, one neither knew the true nor attained penetration into the false.
Now, if one wishes to recognize the principle of delusion, one must also know the truth of the mind;
these each represent one side [of the whole].
Within the detailed explanation:
The former clarifies thorough investigation (*vitarka*),
while the latter clarifies suchness (*yathābhūta*).
Master Jingtong explains as follows:
If one seeks to understand this as it is in reality according to a general explanation,
those above the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) all perform this contemplation;
the stage prior to the grounds can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*):
having already perfected the preceding stage, one transcends into the subsequent stage.
This is also stated as such in the aforementioned text.
One may perform this contemplation during the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) within the intermediate state of indeterminate recording (*avyākṛta-vyākaraṇa*).

However, the text of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explicitly states that such contemplation is cultivated only at the stages of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) and the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*).
Investigation (vitarka) occurs within the roots of goodness of Heat (ūṣmagata) and Peak (mūrdhan);
the four types of knowledge of reality (yathābhūta-jñāna) occur at the stage of Patience (kṣānti), which is foremost.
Investigation has the knowledge of reality as its essential nature.
"Vitarka" (investigation) means seeking;
"vicāra" (analysis) means pondering.
When one seeks and ponders the names, meanings, reality, and falsity, yet has not yet reached a definitive understanding, it is called "vitarka-vicāra" (investigation and analysis).
If determinate knowledge is called "knowledge as-it-is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*),
then thorough investigation (*vitarka*) is the name for its meaning,
while "four" is the name for its number.
This is a designation based on the number and its corresponding meaning,
termed the "four thorough investigations" (catasraḥ paryeṣaṇāḥ) and the "four suchnesses" (catasro yathābhūtaparijñāḥ).
If explained individually according to their respective names:
The investigation of names is itself the object;
"investigation" (vitarka) has the meaning of seeking or searching.
The name is designated based on the meaning of the object.
The same applies to obtaining a name through the investigation of phenomena (*vastu-paryeṣaṇā*).
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the substance;
that which is mutually adventitious is termed "provisionally established" (*prajñapti*).
All conceptual investigations of provisional designations consist of both objects and names;
that is, they are named according to their essential nature and meaning.
This refers to the conceptual investigation of the provisional designation of intrinsic nature.
Regarding the investigation of the designation of distinctions:
one contemplates that names, objects, and so forth each possess specific distinctions such as suffering and impermanence, or being with outflows and without outflows;
"distinction" is the meaning [of this term].
The provisional designations of "investigation" (*vitarka*) and "analysis" (*vicāra*) are names derived from their meanings;
the names for the four [remaining] "as-it-is-realizations" (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*) may be understood by analogy with this.
Thus stated by Dharma Master Tai.
*Vitarka* (本音毘恒迦) is translated here as "investigation" (*xúnsī*).
*Vicāra* (遮羅) is translated as "analysis" (*sì*).
*Bodhi* (菩提) means "awakening" (*jué*).
Vipaśyanā is translated as "contemplation" (guān).
Master Ji says:
"That investigative wisdom which accords with reality (yathābhūta-jñāna) penetrates both types of wisdom."
Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*,
"seeing only names as names and seeing only things as things," Jing says:
Ordinary beings falsely cling to the notion that names belong to objects and objects belong to names,
thinking that wherever there is a name, there must necessarily be an object;
such clinging is the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).
The Bodhisattva contemplates that names are merely provisional designations;
if one seeks the referent through the name, it can never be found.
Therefore, when contemplating the name, one sees only the phenomenon of the name, which is itself its substance.
It is also called "meaning.
When a bodhisattva contemplates the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), they see that these are beyond words;
even when names are provisionally established, they are fundamentally not congruent with their referents.
Therefore, one perceives only the phenomenon and does not perceive the existence of a name.
Tai says:
"Regarding the name, one perceives only the name."
There are two interpretations from the West.
The first states:
regarding names, one perceives only the nature of discrimination as being without intrinsic substance.
The second explanation states:
regarding names, one perceives only the name of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) and does not perceive the name of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
The two interpretations regarding "seeing only the thing within the thing" are likewise similar.
Ce (Cè) states:
"In this contemplation of vitarka and vicāra, one sees only the dependent nature appearing as names."
The word "only" (kevala) serves to distinguish this from the view of outsiders who perceive reality as consisting of names;
thus it says, "only seeing names.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
In this context, "name" refers to form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth;
it also includes the causes of names, the fruits of names, phrases, and so on.
One investigates that these names are of the nature of mere mental verbalization and are merely appearances, not realities.
Not to be separated from mental verbalization is the investigation of names (*nāma-paryeṣaṇā*).
Regarding the inclusion [of this] within the investigation of things (*vastu-paryeṣaṇā*), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states:
"Just as the referents expressed by name-groups (*nāmakāya*) and so forth..."
One investigates by means of the aggregates, elements, and bases;
this nature is merely conventional, neither real nor possessing any distinct categories of existence.
Now, one considers the principle of the correspondence and non-correspondence between such signified objects and their signifiers.
Therefore, it need not be argued that one "investigates.
According to this text, both names and meanings are merely conventionally established.
One contemplates these as they manifest as external-like appearances.
"Reality exists only within.
Regarding the statement, "conventionally designating 'only seeing intrinsic nature' with respect to intrinsic nature," Jing says:
When one contemplates both name and referent together, neither possesses intrinsic nature;
they are mutually adventitious and are thus termed "provisionally established. Why is this so?
If one assumes that names and conventions do not function within that object,
then the name is said to be adventitious with respect to the object;
since its nature transcends speech, it is not of the category of names.
The two objects of observation are called "guests" because they are mutually guests;
both are termed "provisionally established.
Furthermore, this third [mode] is also called the simultaneous contemplation of the ultimate and the conventional.
The name is the conventional;
the meaning is the ultimate. Why is this so?
Because names are merely conventional constructs grasped through one's own conceptualization, they belong to the level of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The dependent and perfected natures, being beyond verbal expression, are the phenomena of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-dharma*).
To now examine them in conjunction is precisely to contemplate both the two truths of the real and the conventional simultaneously.
Ce says: As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains, one investigates the two kinds of self-nature—name and object—as being merely conventionally established characteristics;
that is to say, the self-nature of names and objects such as "form" (*rūpa*) and "feeling" (*vedanā*).
"In reality there is nothing at all, yet its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is provisionally established.
The explanation says:
"It is like the provisional establishment of a person (pudgala)."
Regarding the phrase "only seeing the conventional designations of distinctions within the conventional designations of distinctions," Jing says:
"This refers to observing collectively that names and meanings each possess numerous distinctions, such as being with-outflow (*sāsrava*) or without-outflow (*anāsrava*)."
Therefore, it is said that the provisional establishment of distinctions is the same as before.
To be mutually guests of one another is what is termed "provisional establishment.
The observation of the absence of characteristics refers to the two preceding observations.
The "contemplation of combined characteristics" refers to the latter two contemplations.
Cei states: "As it is said in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*."
The two types of distinctions—namely, those of name (*nāman*) and meaning (*artha*)—are also conventionally established characteristics (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*).
Question: Why are the first two [distinctions] described only as the "intrinsic nature distinction" (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) of names and things, and not termed "conventionally established"?
The commentary states:
The first two contemplations are called "contemplation of the differentiation of names and meanings.
Because they are contemplations that transcend characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are not termed "provisionally established" (*prajñapti*).
Because one contemplates the characteristics of the combination of intrinsic nature and its distinctions,
both name and object are mutually adventitious; therefore,
the latter two are both said to be "provisionally established."
Now, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
these four types are all merely provisional designations. Thus,
that treatise states:
Whether as names or as meanings, both their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and their specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*) are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
Furthermore, according to the *Tripiṭaka* and as stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are two kinds [of observation],
namely the four types of contemplation, as cited in the preceding text.
Alternatively, one may perform six kinds of contemplation.
Thus, that treatise states:
"Whether it be the name or the referent, the self-nature or the distinction, the conventionally established self-nature or the conventionally established distinction."
Since these six kinds of meanings all do not exist, the explanation states:
first, name; second, meaning; third, the self-nature of the name; fourth, the self-nature of the meaning; fifth, the differentiation of the name; and sixth, the differentiation of the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the conventional designation of intrinsic nature and its distinctions," this is a re-explanation of the expression "conventional designation of intrinsic nature and its distinctions.
Next, the four types of knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) are explained.
In the commentary on the "knowledge of reality as it is regarding the foremost," Jing says:
"As for the statement that 'the bodhisattvas, having investigated names, [realize] there is only form,' this refers back to the preceding preparatory practice."
Regarding the provisional designation of names upon things:

this refers to how Bodhisattvas, as they truly understand, know that worldly beings designate such names for such meanings upon things, so that beings may give rise to perceptions and views, and based on those views, engage in verbal expression.

He thoroughly understands the intentions with which sentient beings engage in verbal expression, teaching one another so that the world, by means of speech, gives rise to conceptualizations; by means of conceptualization, gives rise to views; and by means of views, gives rise to further discourse.
Therefore, conventional designations are provisionally established for those phenomena.
This concludes the explanation by way of direct affirmation; hereafter follows the explanation by way of negation.
Even down to the point where there has been no verbal expression since the beginning,
if one can apply this concluding summary,
one will understand the intention with which all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas give rise to their teachings.
How could it be that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, for the sake of causing the world to give rise to the grasping of augmentation,
have spoken with the intention of making known that Bodhisattvas understand the world and sentient beings exactly as they are?
Cè says: "The statement 'such is called [a name] for such a meaning, which is provisionally established upon a thing,' etc.,
clarifies the reason why the dependent nature is provisionally designated by names."
If one were to explain the fault of not establishing [the stages] below all levels such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth,

it should be understood that the wisdom of reality (*yathābhūtajñāna*) clarified here has a mode of activity (*ākāra*) similar to that of the preceding investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*).
The dependent-imagined (paratantra-parikalpita) is based on conditions and is merely provisional, while the imagined (parikalpita) is based on conditions and is non-existent;
these are divided into two categories solely in terms of cause and effect, as well as being determinate or indeterminate.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

During the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), the analytical investigation that seeks to realize that which exists nominally and is non-existent in reality—employing the signs of skillful means—is called "investigation" (*vitarka*).

The knowledge of skillful means that results from this, characterized by the certainty of having realized that which exists nominally and is non-existent in reality, is called "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
It is further stated:
"To investigate that each [phenomenon] is merely conventionally existent and that its substantial reality cannot be found is called 'investigation' (vitarka).
When, upon the arising of this resultant wisdom, one definitively knows that it is conventionally existent and substantially non-existent, this is called 'wisdom as it truly is' (yathābhūta-jñāna)."
Regarding the second, *yathābhūtajñāna* (knowledge of things as they truly are), Jing says:
"One contemplates and perceives all imagined objects, such as form and so forth, which depend upon the other-dependent and perfected natures;
their nature is free from names and words, and thus language cannot reach them."
Ce says: This means that one contemplates the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its ineffable object through the contemplation of reality (*yathābhūta-pratyavekṣā*),
and does not contemplate the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as being truly existent.
Regarding the third point, *yathābhūta* (as it truly is),
Jingyun states: "The statement that 'the *yathābhūta* penetrates contradiction and reaches [the limit],
such that the self-nature of those phenomena appears' clarifies that the *paratantra* (dependent nature) is like a magical illusion— non-existent yet appearing as if existent."
Therefore, it is said that what is not that intrinsic nature appears as that intrinsic nature.

Alternatively, phenomena produced through dependent causes and conditions do not possess the real intrinsic nature as grasped by the deluded minds of ordinary beings, yet they appear as if they possessed that grasped real intrinsic nature.
Therefore, it is said that what is not its own intrinsic nature appears as if it were its own intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, one can discern that those dependent phenomena appear in a manner similar to magical illusions and the like, yet they do not possess that [illusory] essence.
Phenomena arising through causes and conditions exist like illusions or transformations,
yet they differ from those [entities] clung to as having a real substantial nature.
If one can thus understand them as they truly are, and so forth...
The principle of causes and conditions is shallow and beyond the comprehension of ordinary sentiments;
only the Buddha has reached its ultimate realization, and thus it is called most profound.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
Among the Buddha’s ten powers, the power of karma is the most profound.
Cè (Ce) says:
"Furthermore, it is like transformations and the like, which appear real but are not actually so."
This refers to the eight similes as explained in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*.
It is precisely the dependent nature (*paratantra*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The eight similes illustrate the dependent nature" means that the dependent [similes] are used as metaphors for the dependent-arising nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Regarding the fourth [type of] knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), Jing says:
"For instance, a single form is the meaning of non-duality—being neither existent nor non-existent.
Within this dharma of a single form, the form that is conceptually imputed (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is of a non-existent nature."
The dependent nature of form is not non-existent.
These two meanings taken together—being neither existent nor non-existent—are called "non-duality.
Because the imputed nature conforms to verbal expression and lacks substantial reality, it is not existent.
Because the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is established as being beyond verbal expression, it is not non-existent;
this clarifies non-duality by way of its being neither existent nor non-existent.
Next, by way of the two truths, it clarifies non-duality by showing that it is neither material nor immaterial.
This means that because this form, which is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*), is empty,
it is explained as being non-existent in terms of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). However,
because this dependent form (*paratantra-rūpa*) exists as a phenomenon produced by causes and conditions, it does exist.
According to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it is not that form does not exist;
however, in terms of the principle of thorough conceptualization (parikalpita-svabhāva), even according to the conventional truth, form has no substantial essence.
Now, I shall compose this with alternating phrasing.
Therefore, it is only within the context of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) that one speaks of non-existence.
Even if form (*rūpa*) produced from dependent causes and conditions (*paratantra*) were to exist within ultimate truth, it would not be negated;
for principle and phenomenon proceed together without mutual obstruction.
This is also composed with elegant literary artistry;
it merely clarifies, from the perspective of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), that things are not non-existent.
One should understand through the two preceding sections the meaning of the non-duality of existence and non-existence, as well as seeing and non-seeing.
This means that when the dependent nature of form possesses substantial existence, it can serve as a condition for the occurrence of seeing;
whereas the imagined nature of form lacks substantial existence and cannot serve as a condition for the occurrence of seeing—this is called "seeing the non-existent."
One may also say that the text is abbreviated;
in full, it should state: "visible and non-visible, non-visible and non-non-visible.
This passage is explained by relying on the principle of the two natures to clarify non-duality.
Ce says: "The statement that those various phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent means that,

upon emerging from contemplation, one perceives that the objects of the境 (viṣaya) are conventionally existent as dependent origination (paratantra), yet lack the characteristics of being either existent or non-existent."
Regarding the statement that "because the nature of being expressible is not established as real, it is not existent,
etc.," this clarifies that the dependent nature is non-existent because it is devoid of the expressible parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature).
Because it exists dependently upon causes and conditions apart from verbal expression, it is not non-existent by nature.

Thus, the statement that "in terms of ultimate truth, there is no form and so forth" means that within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because of its perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the imagined form (*parikalpita-rūpa*) is absent; therefore, it is said that there is no form.
Because form is conventionally designated as existing within the dependent conventional truth, it is not non-form.
Third, it clarifies that because the wisdom of the deluded is deficient, they give rise to conceptual construction, and thus the cycle of transmigration flows on without ceasing.

The statement, "It is said that by means of such false conceptualizations, various defilements arise and one wanders through birth and death," indicates that these eight types of false conceptualization are merely skillful means.

From these eight types of conceptualization within the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the fundamental afflictions (*kleśa*)—the dual grasping at persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*) as well as the three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion—arise.
Fourth, because the bodhisattva relies on wisdom to comprehend conceptualization, they are able to realize the great fruit.
Within this, there are four sections.
First, it clarifies that the bodhisattva is able to extinguish conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and attain great nirvāṇa.
Second, it clarifies the attainment of various masteries (*vaśitā*).
The three vidyās can attain five benefits and five activities;
the four vidyās encompass all that is to be accomplished through five kinds of supreme advantages.
The first [passage] states that by relying on these four types of knowledge as it truly is, a bodhisattva is even able to realize the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Jingyun: The Bodhisattva, dwelling in the present, knows the faults of discrimination through knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and does not give rise to discrimination.
Because he does not give rise to discrimination, he does not perfuse the seeds of the objective conditions upon which he relies.
Therefore, in future lives, conditioned by dependence, [phenomena] will not arise.
Because they do not arise in future lives through dependence on conditions, the conceptual discrimination that would otherwise arise from those dependent conditions should likewise not arise.
Because both such conceptual discrimination and its objective basis have ceased, one realizes great *nirvāṇa*.
Cè states: "This clarifies the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇa-sampad*)."

The second explanation below concerns the attainment of mastery through knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Within this present life, one attains all forms of mastery and so forth. This concludes the second explanation.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, a general statement;
second, a detailed analysis.
The final summary is the most excellent.
Regarding the specific analysis, there are four [points].
The first is the attainment of the mastery of prophecy, transformation, and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Second, one attains mastery over transformation.
Jing says:
"Transformation is the characteristic of the fruit of supernormal power."
This is also called mastery over supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vaśitā*),
which is common to the Hīnayāna.

However, in the Hīnayāna, the fourteen minds of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and are bound to both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The Mahāyāna is wholesome and exists exclusively in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
however, because its activities resemble those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is also called the desire realm.
This capacity for transformation is the pervasive essence.
The subsequent text will explain these two masteries.
Third, one attains mastery over wisdom regarding all objects.
Fourth, one attains mastery over the maintenance or relinquishment of the life-span.
Ce says:
This clarifies that because wisdom is pure, one attains three kinds of mastery.
The first is mastery over supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Second is mastery over knowledge;
third is mastery over life.
Among the ten masteries, the remaining seven are omitted here for brevity.

In this way, the bodhisattva even attains five kinds of supreme benefits and so forth; this concludes the third section clarifying that by attaining mastery, one obtains five benefits and performs five activities.
First, the five benefits are clarified.
First is attaining tranquility of mind.
*Ce* (Cai) says:
Because one attains the four kinds of wisdom that dwell in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*), one is able to eliminate the heaviness (*dausthulya*) of body and mind.
First, because they are inwardly concentrated, they do not sever their afflictions;
second, their sublime wisdom and vision operate within the fields of knowledge;
third, they never grow weary of the cyclic existence of sentient beings.
Fourth, one is able to skillfully enter the meaning of the Tathāgata’s intentional terminology.
Fifth, one attains resolute conviction in the Mahāyāna such that it cannot be diverted by false conditions.
Ce (Cesheng) says:
The first three constitute the victory of self-perfection;
the latter two constitute the victory of further advancement.
Within the first three, the first clarifies meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the next wisdom (*jñāna*), and the last compassion (*karuṇā*).
Of the latter two [sections], the first clarifies the excellence of penetrating the noble teachings;
the second clarifies the excellence of possessing supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) capable of defeating non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*);
and the next clarifies the five activities (*pañcakarma*).
Each [point] has two parts:
first, the clarification of the characteristics of the activity;
second, from "it should be known" onwards, the conclusion that it belongs to the superior benefits.
This fourth activity is able to eliminate the doubts and confusions arising in others,
causing them to understand the Buddha-dharma and transmit it from one to another;
that is to say, it protects and sustains the Tathāgata’s sublime and correct Dharma-eye, enabling it to endure for a long time.
If false teachings disrupt the truth,
the Bodhisattva is able to discern the true from the counterfeit; therefore,
it is said that regarding the semblance of the True Dharma which can obscure the Tathāgata’s holy teaching, they know how to reveal, rectify, and eliminate it.
Thus, having concluded the fourth section, this clarifies how the five benefits encompass all that is to be accomplished,
first in general and then in detail;
within the detailed explanation, there are five phrases.
First, personal peace and happiness free from defilement;
second, the accomplishment of the Buddha-dharma;
third, the accomplishment of sentient beings.
Fourth, protecting the correct and crushing the heterodox.
Fifth, being diligent, courageous, and unwavering in right aspiration.
From here below begins the third major section, which concludes the formation of the three categories.
Because the objects of knowledge vary in their depth and shallowness, the cognizing wisdom that apprehends them is likewise established as three grades.
That is to say, first is the worldly consensus reality (*lokaprasiddha-tattva*),
which corresponds to the worldly cognition of the four great elements, the five sense objects, armies, forests, suffering, confinement, and so forth.
Second is the reality established through universally accepted reasoning (*yukti-siddha-tattva*).
By means of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one establishes what is correct and refutes what is erroneous through this reasoning.
Since both the objects and the cognitions of these two belong to the stage of the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), they are inferior.
Therefore, the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states:
"The first two realities are subsumed under the conceptualization of names and signs (*nāma-nimitta-vikalpa*).
The third—the objective realm of the wisdom purified of the afflictive obscurations—is the suchness (*tathatā*) manifested by the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*)."

This fourth object of knowledge within the intermediate category—the sphere of wisdom purified of cognitive obstructions—is precisely the suchness revealed by the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Because its principle has been transformed into something pure and sublime, it is classified as "superior.
Thus, the *Viniścaya* states:
The latter two realities are subsumed within correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*).
